Chapter 1 Strain

1.18 Do the strains fit together

In section 1.17 we computed from the displacement field of a body how the material is strained close to each point. When the partial derivatives of the displacements are small, in absolute value for example at most \(0{,}001\), the quadratic part of the Green-Lagrange tensor is at most \(1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and we neglect it (section 1.17.3, figure 1.392). Then the strain is described by six numbers, the components of the small strain tensor ((1.51)): three normal strains and three shear strains. When the derivatives are not small, we need the whole Green-Lagrange tensor (note 4 at the end of the section). Let us write the components of the small strain tensor once more:

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\Big) . \end{aligned} \tag{1.63}\]

Let us draw what these equations say. The left rectangle contains the three components of the displacement, \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\). The right rectangle contains the six components of the strain, three normal ones at the top and three shear ones at the bottom. The blue arrow labelled \(\partial\) above them points from the left rectangle to the right one, because we get the strains from the displacements by differentiation according to (1.63). The lines between the rectangles say which displacement component appears in which strain. The grey lines lead from \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The blue ones lead from \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). The blackwhite ones lead from \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\). So each displacement component appears in three strains. Two lines lead to each shear strain, because it is half the sum of the derivatives of two displacement components. The grey dashed arrow with a question mark below the rectangles points back, because this is the opposite question of this section, which we cannot answer yet.

On the right-hand sides only three functions, the displacement components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) appear, while on the left there are six. In this section we ask the opposite question. If six functions are given, is there a displacement field from which we get them by (1.63)? We will see that there is not always one. Six functions that come from three cannot be arbitrary: they must satisfy six equations. The path to them and beyond:

  1. On the example of a strip we look at how strains can fail to fit together (section 1.18.1).
  2. We meet derivatives of partial derivatives and show that for them the order in which we differentiate does not matter (section 1.18.2).
  3. With this we derive the six equations and say what they mean (section 1.18.3).
  4. Later, in section 1.18.4, we show that the strains determine the displacements exactly up to a shift and a small rotation of the body.
  5. Later we also look at when the equations are enough for a displacement field to exist, and in section 1.18.5 why they are not enough for a body with a hole.

1.18.1 Six functions from three

Why would anyone know the strains but not the displacements? In this chapter we always went from displacements to strains. In chapter 3, though, we will learn how the strain of a piece of material depends on the forces acting on it, and on whether it is heated. Then we will often know the strains before the displacements. In a body that is heated unevenly, for instance, every piece wants to stretch in its own way, as much as it was heated. If these stretches do not fit together, the pieces cannot stretch as they would like to, and they push on each other or pull on each other. So we must be able to check whether prescribed strains fit together.

For the bar this question did not come up. There the strain was a single function \(\varepsilon(x)\), and we get the displacement of a point by adding up the elongations of all pieces from the held end to the point (we will write this precisely in section 3.5). For a constant strain \(\varepsilon_0\) we divide the bar from \(0\) to \(x\) into \(n\) pieces of length \(\Delta x = x/n\). Each gets longer by \(\varepsilon_0\,\Delta x\), as the vertical sides of the blue triangles under the graph \(u(x) = \varepsilon_0\,x\) in figure 1.47 show, so

\[u(x) = n\,\varepsilon_0\,\Delta x = \varepsilon_0\,x .\]

The pieces of the bar lie in one row, and each touches only the previous one and the next one. When a piece gets longer, it only pushes all the following ones forward, so the pieces of the bar fit together for every function \(\varepsilon(x)\). In the plane and in space, though, every piece has neighbours in several directions, and three functions give six. This is the reason why the six functions cannot be arbitrary.

What it means that strains do not fit together is easiest to picture like this (CM §3.7.1, PDF p. 149). Before loading we cut the body into small cubes. In figure 1.428 the cubes are drawn as squares, six in two rows, in blackwhite. The blue point \(A\) is a corner shared by four neighbouring squares. We strain each cube separately as the given strains prescribe, and then try to put the cubes back together into a whole body. The deformation is greatly magnified in the figure. In the middle every piece is lengthened in orange in the direction of the axis \(x\) by the same fraction, a quarter, and the pieces fit together without gaps. The point \(A\) is a single point also after the deformation. On the right the bottom row does not get longer, while the top row gets longer by a half. This is how the pieces would want to stretch if we heated the top row and not the bottom one. Each row by itself fits together, like the pieces of the bar. But the two thickly drawn sides that should touch have different lengths, the bottom one has three sides of a square, the top one four and a half. The top row is raised only so that the two sides do not overlap in the figure.

Why can we not simply shift the top row so that the pieces touch only partly? Because the point \(A\) before the deformation was a single point of the body, shared by the bottom and the top piece. By definition 1.23 a displacement field assigns to every point a single displacement. On the right, though, \(A\) is in one place as a corner of the bottom piece and in another as a corner of the top piece, so the same point would get two different displacements. If the strains are arbitrary, the cubes do not fit together without gaps or overlaps. They fit only if the strain of every cube agrees with the strains of its neighbours: the common sides of neighbouring pieces must have the same length after the deformation and must coincide, so that every point has a single displacement. For a strip cut into bands of squares we will see both in figure 1.431.

Let us try this on an example. A thin steel strip of length 200 mm and height 20 mm lies in a plane in which we place the axes \(x\) and \(y\) (figure 1.429). The axis \(x\) points along the strip, the axis \(y\) across it, and the origin is at the middle of the left end. So the strip reaches from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 200\) mm and from \(y = -10\) mm to \(y = 10\) mm. No force acts on it. This is a thought experiment: we prescribe a strain to every piece of the strip and ask whether the strip as a whole can take it. Let us prescribe

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0 , \tag{1.64}\]

and let the other three components be zero. Why exactly \(y^2\)? The strain that changes uniformly with height, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\) with a constant length \(R\), we will try below for comparison, and there the pieces fit together. The function \(y^2\) is the simplest one that does not change uniformly with height: from \(y = 0\) to \(5\) mm it grows by \(25\) mm², and from \(5\) to \(10\) mm by \(75\) mm². This is how the pieces would want to shorten if we cooled the strip more at the edges than in the middle. The number \(k\) is a constant. Since \(y^2\) has the unit m² and a strain has no unit, \(k\) has the unit m⁻². Let us take \(k = -10\) m⁻², so that the strains at the edges are a thousandth in size, which by section 1.1 is the upper limit for the strains of steel structures. The longitudinal fibre in the middle of the strip, where \(y = 0\), is to keep its length. The longitudinal fibres at the edges, where \(y = \pm 10\) mm, are to shorten by \(10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}01\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}001\), by a thousandth. The fibres at the height \(y = \pm 5\) mm are to shorten by \(10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}005\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}00025\), four times less, because \(y\) is half as large there and so \(y^2\) is four times smaller. The prescribed strains of the five fibres drawn in figure 1.429 are therefore:

height \(y\) \(-10\) mm \(-5\) mm \(0\) \(5\) mm \(10\) mm
\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) \(-0{,}001\) \(-0{,}00025\) \(0\) \(-0{,}00025\) \(-0{,}001\)

Let us draw this as we would on a board. On the left is the blackwhite rectangle, the strip before deformation, with five horizontal lines, which are the longitudinal fibres at the heights \(-10\), \(-5\), \(0\), \(5\) and \(10\) mm. The strip is drawn proportionally shorter and taller than in reality, so that it can be drawn. The axis \(x\) points along the strip, the axis \(y\) across it. The heights of the fibres in millimetres are written at their left ends. We then draw each fibre also after the deformation, in orange, from the same left end. A short transverse tick marks the end of the shortened fibre, and the blackwhite remainder shows by how much it has shortened. The fibre in the middle does not shorten, so the orange line reaches the right edge. The fibres at \(y = \pm 5\) mm shorten by \(0{,}00025\), the fibres at the edges by \(0{,}001\). The shortening is greatly magnified in the figure: at the edges it is drawn as a quarter of the length instead of a thousandth, so that it can be seen. So the differences between the fibres are visible, although in reality they are tiny.

On the right is the graph of the strain. The horizontal axis is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the vertical one is the height \(y\) with the same scale as the strip, so the fibres and the points of the graph are at the same height. The labels on the vertical axis are heights in millimetres. The blue parabola is the prescribed strain \(k\,y^2\). Its vertex is at \(y = 0\), because the strain is zero there, and it opens to the left, because \(k\) is negative. On it are the five blue dots, the values of the five fibres from the table. The horizontal grey dashed lines lead from the dots to the axis \(y\), so that it can be seen at which height each dot lies. The vertical grey dashed lines lead from the dots down to the values below the graph, \(-0{,}001\) at \(y = \pm 10\) mm and \(-0{,}00025\) at \(y = \pm 5\) mm.

Let us look at a small piece of the strip at the top edge, just below the fibre at the height \(10\) mm. The blackwhite piece is before the deformation, \(\Delta x\) long and \(\Delta y\) high. The orange piece is after the deformation. The longitudinal sides are \(\Delta x\,(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\) long: the original length \(\Delta x\) gets the elongation \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\Delta x\), which is negative here because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} < 0\), so the sides are shorter. The transverse sides keep the length \(\Delta y\), because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), and the right angles between longitudinal and transverse sides stay right, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). The shortening is greatly magnified in the figure.

Do the pieces strained in this way fit together into a strip? Let us draw what we will do. The blackwhite grid on the left is the strip before deformation, cut into five horizontal bands of five squares. The axis \(x\) points along the bands, the axis \(y\) upwards. The strip is proportionally shortened in the figure. The bands are 4 mm high and the strip is 200 mm long, so in reality each band would have 50 squares with a side of 4 mm. The strip in the middle is for comparison, with the deformation written by the label above it, which we prescribe below. On the right the strip in orange has every band deformed by (1.64), with the strain \(k\,y^2\) at the heights that the band covers. The deformation is greatly magnified in the figure, so that it can be seen. We placed all the bands one on top of another at the left end, so that they touch there. The band is 4 mm high, so the strain changes also within the band. For the band between \(y = 2\) mm and \(y = 6\) mm the edges shorten by

\[\begin{aligned} &\text{top edge: } 10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}006\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}00036 , \\ &\text{bottom edge: } 10\ \text{m}^{-2} \cdot (0{,}002\ \text{m})^2 = 0{,}00004 . \end{aligned}\]

The shorter upper edge bends the band upward. The bands curve differently, and grey gaps open between them. Why the band curves, instead of staying straight and only being shorter at the top, let us draw on a single piece.

The blackwhite rectangle (1) is a piece of this band before the deformation, \(\Delta x\) wide and \(\Delta y\) high. Its bottom and top sides are short longitudinal fibres at the heights \(y\) and \(y + \Delta y\), which start at the same transverse fibre, the left edge. The orange piece is after the deformation, as it would be if the longitudinal fibres stayed horizontal. We leave the left edge in place, because we look only at how the piece deforms relative to its left edge. After the deformation a fibre has the length \(\Delta x\,(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\), as for the piece at the edge of the strip, the lower one \(\Delta x\,\big(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y)\big)\), the upper one \(\Delta x\,\big(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y + \Delta y)\big)\). The four grey dashed lines carry the ends of the fibres to the grey dimensions. The upper fibre shortens more, so the right edge is tilted: its upper end is to the left of the lower end by the difference of the two lengths, at the height \(\Delta y\). The transverse fibre therefore tilts to the left by

\[\frac{\Delta x\,\big(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y)\big) - \Delta x\,\big(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y + \Delta y)\big)}{\Delta y} = -\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y + \Delta y) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y)}{\Delta y}\,\Delta x\]

horizontal distance per unit of height. The deformation is greatly magnified in the figure.

But right angles stay right, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), as for the piece at the edge. The orange piece (2) is therefore drawn so that all four of its angles are right. The right edge is tilted as in (1), by the angle \(\varphi\) from the grey dashed vertical. The right angle between the right edge and the fibre rotates as a whole, so the fibre at the right edge must also rotate, by the same angle \(\varphi\) from the grey dashed horizontal. At the left edge the fibres are horizontal, at the right edge rotated by \(\varphi\), so in between they are curved, upward, because the right edge tilted to the left. Since the angle at the edge and at the fibre is the same, the fibre rises per unit of length by as much as the edge moves to the left per unit of height. The slope of the longitudinal fibre therefore changes over the length \(\Delta x\) by the tilt of the right edge, and for a small piece this is almost equal to the number from the display above.

The next piece in the row starts at the rotated right edge of the previous one and rotates by the same angle again. On the right (3) there are four pieces in a row in blackwhite before the deformation. The orange curves are the lower and upper longitudinal fibre of the row after the deformation. The upper one shortens more than the lower one, so the curves are arcs around the same centre above the row. The orange transverse lines are the transverse fibres. They stay perpendicular to the longitudinal fibres, so each is tilted more than the previous one. The row curves upward, and the more, the larger the difference of the strains of the upper and lower fibre per unit of height.

This is how every band of the right strip curves. The band in the middle stays straight, because its edges at \(y = \pm 2\) mm shorten equally. The bands above it curve upward, the bands below it downward, because for them the lower edge shortens more. The farther from the middle a band lies, the larger the difference of the shortenings of its edges and the more it curves. So gaps open between the bands, and they get wider and wider towards the right end. The pieces do not fit together.

For comparison, the strip in the middle of figure 1.431 prescribes the strain

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{y}{R} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0 , \qquad R = 10\ \text{m} ,\]

and the other components zero. The longitudinal fibres above the middle get longer and those below it shorter, in proportion to the distance from the middle, at the edges by a thousandth, since \(0{,}01\ \text{m} / 10\ \text{m} = 0{,}001\). Here all bands curve in the same way, like parts of rings around the same centre, and they fit together without gaps. A bent horizontal bar, which we will treat in chapter 5, curves in a similar way.

What is \(R\)? Let us draw the longitudinal fibres as arcs around the same centre. The point \(O\) is the centre, below the strip. The middle fibre is an arc with the radius \(R\), between the two grey dashed radii with the angle \(\theta\). Its length is \(R\,\theta\), as much as before the deformation, because the middle fibre does not get longer. The fibre at the height \(y\) above it is an arc with the same angle, with the radius larger by \(y\). Its length is \((R + y)\,\theta\), and before the deformation it was as long as the middle fibre. Its strain is therefore

\[\frac{(R + y)\,\theta - R\,\theta}{R\,\theta} = \frac{y}{R} .\]

So the number \(R\) is the radius of the arc into which the middle fibre curves. At \(R = 10\) m the centre is 10 m below the strip, and in the figure it is brought much closer.

For the second strip a displacement field exists. Let us find it. By (1.63) the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) must satisfy three equations, for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\):

\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} = \frac{y}{R} , \qquad \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} = 0 , \qquad \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} = 0 .\]

We compute partial derivatives as ordinary derivatives in which the other variables are treated as numbers, with the rules of lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation. We solve the equations one by one, each time with the simplest function that satisfies it.

  1. The function \(x\,y/R\) has the derivative \(y/R\) with respect to \(x\), since \(y/R\) is a constant number there. Let us take \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = x\,y/R\), and the first equation holds.
  2. The derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(y\) is \(x/R\). For the right angles to stay right, by the second equation \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = -x/R\) is needed. The function \(-x^2/(2R)\) has such a derivative with respect to \(x\), so let us take \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -x^2/(2R)\).
  3. This \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) does not depend on \(y\), so \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = 0\), and the third equation holds.

So the field is

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{x\,y}{R} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -\frac{x^2}{2R} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 .\]

The component \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) is zero, and \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) do not depend on \(z\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are also zero, as we prescribed.

The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -x^2/(2R)\) is the vertical displacement of a point of the longitudinal fibre that was at \(x\) before the deformation. The graph of the function \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) against \(x\) is therefore the shape of the fibre after the deformation. In figure 1.433 on the right, the horizontal axis is \(x\) from \(0\) to \(200\) mm, and the vertical one is \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) in millimetres, stretched 40 times more. The orange curve is the graph of \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -x^2/(2R)\). Since \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) does not depend on the height \(y\), this is the shape of all longitudinal fibres: they all curve the same way, and that is exactly why the bands in the middle fit together. On the left, the two arcs are curved differently, because there \(y\) is drawn as a third of \(R\). In reality \(y\) is at most 10 mm and \(R\) is 10 m, and the radii differ only by a thousandth. The right end of the strip at \(x = 0{,}2\) m drops by \(0{,}2^2/(2 \cdot 10)\ \text{m} = 0{,}002\) m, by 2 mm.

For the first strip, though, we will not find such a field. Before we show this, let us write down precisely what we are looking for.

Definition 1.123 Compatible strains (kompatibilne deformacije)

Let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) be functions of three variables defined at the interior points of a body. These functions are compatible strains (kompatibilne deformacije) if there is a continuously differentiable displacement field \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) (definition 1.90), defined at the same points, such that the equations (1.63) hold at each of them.

Source: BARBER §2.2.1 (PDF p. 46), CM §3.7.1 (PDF p. 149).

The word compatibility means the ability to go together: strains are compatible if the strained pieces go together into a whole body. Then every point has a single displacement, like the point \(A\) in the middle of figure 1.428. For pieces that do not fit together the same point would get two displacements, while by definition 1.23 a displacement field assigns to every point a single displacement vector. The strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\) are compatible, since we found a displacement field for them. For the strains (1.64) we will show in section 1.18.3 that they are not.

Why do the bands of the first strip curve differently (figure 1.431, right)? On the row of pieces of figure 1.432 we saw that the fibres curve when the strain changes with height, and the faster it changes, the more. For the first strip it changes at different heights at different rates. To write this precisely we need the derivative of a partial derivative and the fact that it does not matter in which order we differentiate twice.

1.18.2 Second partial derivatives

Let us return to the hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a diameter of 10 mm hangs and stretches under its own weight. It is held in an idealized way: only the point \(O\) at the centre of the top end is fixed, and the weight is carried by a force spread evenly over the top face. The axis \(x\) points from \(O\) vertically down, the axis \(y\) and the axis \(z\) lie horizontally. By (1.18) the displacement field is

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z) &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \qquad a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} . \end{aligned}\]

We will look mainly at the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), the displacement in the direction of the axis \(y\). By the table in section 1.7.2 its partial derivatives with respect to \(y\) and to \(x\) are

\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(x, y, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) , \qquad \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}(x, y, z) = 0{,}6\,a\,y .\]

Let us draw the bar, seen from the side. The blackwhite rectangle is the bar before loading. The hatched line above it is the ceiling that carries the bar. The top face is not glued to it. It is carried by a distributed force, which is not drawn, so the face can narrow. The blackwhite dot on it is the fixed point \(O\). The arrow pointing down at the top left shows the direction of the axis \(x\), and the arrow pointing right the direction of the axis \(y\). The axes go through \(O\), they are drawn at the side so that they do not cover the bar. So the right edge of the bar is at \(y > 0\). The orange line is the outline of the bar after loading. At the top the bar is narrower than at the bottom, because \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y\) is larger in size at smaller \(x\) and is negative at \(y > 0\): the right edge moves towards the axis, and the left edge equally towards the axis from the other side. The narrowing is greatly magnified. In reality the bar at the top gets thinner by only \(0{,}6\,a\,L = 1{,}17 \cdot 10^{-6}\) of its radius, while in the figure it is \(0{,}3\) of the radius, so it is magnified about \(256\,000\) times. We measure the displacement of the right edge at two depths. The grey dimension on the left is the depth \(x\) from the top end, the second grey dimension is the depth \(x + \Delta x\). At each depth the blue arrow shows the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) of the edge. The arrow is short, so a grey dashed line at the same height leads from it to the blue label \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) on the right. The upper arrow is longer than the lower one, because the narrowing is larger at the top.

In section 1.7.3 we saw that the slope \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) at the depth \(x + \Delta x\) is slightly different from that at the depth \(x\), because lower down the bar thins less (figure 1.109). In figure 1.434 we see the slope as the displacement of the right edge. At constant \(x\) the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) is proportional to \(y\), so the displacement of an edge 5 mm from the axis equals the slope multiplied by 5 mm. The displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) at the depth \(x\) is therefore larger in size than the displacement at the depth \(x + \Delta x\). So a partial derivative is again a function of the point, and we can ask how fast it changes as we move. This is a derivative of a derivative. We will need it because the strains are already derivatives of the displacements. The relations between strains that we are looking for will contain derivatives of strains, that is, derivatives of derivatives of displacements.

Let us draw two graphs. On the left, the horizontal axis is the depth \(x\), from the top end to the end of the bar at \(L\), and the vertical axis is the derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\). The blackwhite line is this derivative. At \(x = 0\) it has the value \(-0{,}6\,a\,L\), and at \(x = L\) zero, because \(L - x = 0\) there. It is a line because \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) is a linear function. The blue triangle on the left measures the slope of this line. The horizontal leg is the step \(\Delta x\), and the vertical one is the change of the derivative over this step, \(0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\). The slope is their quotient, \(0{,}6\,a\). On the right graph the horizontal axis is the coordinate \(y\), measured from the axis of the bar, so it runs into negative values too, and the vertical axis is the derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\). The blackwhite line goes through the origin, because \(0{,}6\,a\,y\) is proportional to \(y\). The blue triangle again measures the slope. Its horizontal leg is \(\Delta y\), the vertical one \(0{,}6\,a\,\Delta y\), and the quotient is again \(0{,}6\,a\). The scales on the axes of the two graphs are different: on the left graph the length of the bar, 10 m, is drawn horizontally, and on the right graph, over the same length, its diameter, 10 mm. So we do not compare the slopes by eye but with the triangles: in both the vertical leg is \(0{,}6\,a\) times the horizontal one.

Let us compute how fast \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) changes with depth. In figure 1.435 this is the slope of the left graph. We split the expression \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) into \(-0{,}6\,a\,L + 0{,}6\,a\,x\). The first term is a constant, with derivative zero, and by lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation the second has the derivative \(0{,}6\,a\). So

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\Big) = 0{,}6\,a = 1{,}171 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} .\]

When we go down by 1 m, the slope \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\) grows by \(1{,}171 \cdot 10^{-7}\). Since it is negative, its size decreases: lower down the bar thins less.

Definition 1.124 Second partial derivatives (drugi parcialni odvodi)

Let \(f\) be a function of three variables, and let its partial derivative \(\partial f / \partial x\) exist at all points whose distance from the point \(P\) is less than some number \(r > 0\). Then \(\partial f / \partial x\) is again a function of three variables, defined at these points. Its partial derivative with respect to \(y\) at the point \(P\), if it exists, is the second partial derivative (drugi parcialni odvod) of the function \(f\), first with respect to \(x\) and then with respect to \(y\):

\[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Big)(P) . \tag{1.65}\]

In the same way we define the second partial derivative for every pair of variables from \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), also for a pair of equal variables, which we write \(\partial^2 f / \partial x^2\). A second partial derivative with respect to two different variables is a mixed partial derivative (mešani odvod). Partial derivatives of third order are obtained in the same way from second partial derivatives, for example

\[\frac{\partial^3 f}{\partial z\,\partial y\,\partial x}(P) = \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}\Big)(P) .\]

Source: LEBL2 §8.6 (PDF p. 60), for functions of \(n\) variables and derivatives of any order.

Let us draw the chain of differentiation. The top row starts at the function \(f\). The first blue arrow labelled \(\partial / \partial x\) means differentiation with respect to \(x\) and leads to the derivative \(\partial f / \partial x\). The second blue arrow means differentiation with respect to \(y\) and leads to the second derivative. In the bottom row we start at the same function \(f\), differentiate first with respect to \(y\) to \(\partial f / \partial y\) and then with respect to \(x\) to the second derivative. The top chain is blue, because its result is the derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) from definition 1.124. The bottom chain is blackwhite and has the opposite order. Between the results stands the sign \(= ?\), because we do not yet know whether they are equal.

A second partial derivative at a point is a number. As a function of the point it is again a function of three variables, which we can differentiate further. A function of three variables has nine second partial derivatives, one for each of the nine choices of the first and the second variable. The notation \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) is read from right to left: first we differentiate with respect to the variable standing closest to \(f\), that is \(x\), and then with respect to \(y\). Some books write a mixed derivative with subscripts, \(f_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and then the subscripts stand in the opposite order to our notation (LEBL2, PDF p. 60). As with partial derivatives, we do not use subscripts. The condition that \(\partial f / \partial x\) exists at all points near \(P\) is needed because the definition of the partial derivative 1.25 needs the function \(\partial f / \partial x\) at the points \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + \Delta y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) for all small enough \(\Delta y\).

For the hanging bar we computed above the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\,\partial y = 0{,}6\,a\). Let us compute the other second partial derivatives of the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) too. The derivative in a row is the first derivative, and the column says with respect to which variable we differentiate it the second time. Differentiating \(0{,}6\,a\,y\) with respect to \(y\) gives \(0{,}6\,a\), and with respect to \(x\) and to \(z\) zero, because \(x\) and \(z\) do not appear in the expression. The derivative of \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) with respect to \(x\) we computed above, and with respect to \(y\) and to \(z\) it is zero. The derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z\) is zero at every point, so all its derivatives are zero as well.

w.r.t. \(x\) w.r.t. \(y\) w.r.t. \(z\)
\(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\) \(0\) \(0{,}6\,a\) \(0\)
\(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) \(0{,}6\,a\) \(0\) \(0\)
\(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z = 0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\)

The two mixed derivatives with respect to \(x\) and \(y\) are equal (figure 1.435):

\[\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y\,\partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\big(0{,}6\,a\,y\big) = 0{,}6\,a , \qquad \frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\big(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\big) = 0{,}6\,a .\]

We read the meaning of both in two steps, first the meaning of the first derivative, then the meaning of its derivative:

  • The first derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\) says how fast the displacement toward the axis decreases as we go down. This rate is larger the farther from the axis we are (right graph). The mixed derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\,\partial x = 0{,}6\,a\) says by how much this rate grows per metre of distance from the axis (slope of the right graph).
  • The first derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) says how strongly the bar thins at the depth \(x\) (left graph). The mixed derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\,\partial y = 0{,}6\,a\) says by how much this thinning decreases per metre of depth (slope of the left graph).

So the first mixed derivative measures how the rate of decrease of the displacement changes with the distance from the axis, and the second how the thinning changes with depth. These two changes sound different, yet they are equal. For the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\), too, the two mixed derivatives are equal for each of the three pairs of variables, \(x\) and \(y\), \(x\) and \(z\), and \(y\) and \(z\). For \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) all are zero, because \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) is a sum of a function of \(x\) only, a function of \(y\) only and a function of \(z\) only, for example \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\,\partial x = \partial / \partial y\,\big(2a\,(L - x)\big) = 0\) and \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\,\partial y = \partial / \partial x\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y) = 0\). The component \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z\) is \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(y\) replaced by \(z\). So for it the pair \(x\) and \(z\) is equal to the pair \(x\) and \(y\) for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), with the same slopes, and is not zero:

\[\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z\,\partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\big(0{,}6\,a\,z\big) = 0{,}6\,a , \qquad \frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\big(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\big) = 0{,}6\,a .\]

The other two pairs are zero for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and for \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Is the equality a coincidence? Let us look at four values of a function \(f\) at the corners of a small rectangle whose sides are parallel to the axes \(x\) and \(y\) (figure 1.437). Let the coordinate \(z\) be \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\) everywhere, so we leave it out of the notation and write \(f(x, y)\) instead of \(f(x, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\). The corners are \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\), \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}})\), \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\) and \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\), where \(s\) and \(t\) are positive numbers. We add the values with alternating signs:

\[\begin{aligned} g(s, t) &= f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) \\ &\quad - f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}}) + f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}) . \end{aligned} \tag{1.66}\]

We call the number \(g(s, t)\) the double difference. Let us draw it. The axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(y\) upward. The rectangle has the side \(s\) along \(x\) and the side \(t\) along \(y\). Its four corners are the points at which we take the values of \(f\). The lower left corner is the point \(P\). The grey dashed lines and the marks on the axes show the coordinates of the corners: \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s\) on the axis \(x\), \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t\) on the axis \(y\). The signs beside the corners belong to the values in the equation: plus at \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\), minus at the other two. Two blue arrows outside the top and bottom sides point in the direction of the axis \(x\), because there we will look at the change of \(f\) along \(x\). Two blackwhite arrows outside the right and left sides point in the direction of the axis \(y\) for the same reason. The points \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) inside the rectangle and the grey dashed lines through them we need only in the proof of the theorem below, where we also explain them. The terms can be grouped in two ways.

  1. The first two and the last two: \(\big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\big) - \big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}}) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\big)\). This is the change of \(f\) along the top side, in the direction of the axis \(x\), minus the change along the bottom side (blue arrows in figure 1.437). Divided by \(s\), it gives approximately \(\partial f / \partial x\) at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t\) minus \(\partial f / \partial x\) at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\), the more accurately the smaller \(s\) is. Divided further by \(t\), it gives approximately how fast \(\partial f / \partial x\) changes with \(y\), that is \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\).
  2. The first and the third, and the second and the fourth: \(\big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}})\big) - \big(f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\big)\). This is the change along the right side, in the direction of the axis \(y\), minus the change along the left side (blackwhite arrows). Divided by \(t\) and by \(s\), it is approximately \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\).

So the same number \(g(s, t)/(s\,t)\) approximates both mixed derivatives (the changes along the sides of the rectangle), and we expect them to be equal. For the component \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y\) of the hanging bar, which does not depend on \(z\), the double difference is

\[\begin{aligned} g(s, t) &= -0{,}6\,a\,\big[(L - x_{\mathrm{P}} - s)(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - (L - x_{\mathrm{P}})(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) \\ &\qquad - (L - x_{\mathrm{P}} - s)\,y_{\mathrm{P}} + (L - x_{\mathrm{P}})\,y_{\mathrm{P}}\big] . \end{aligned}\]

In the square bracket the first two terms together give \(-s\,(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\), and the last two give \(s\,y_{\mathrm{P}}\). The sum is \(-s\,t\), so \(g(s, t) = 0{,}6\,a\,s\,t\) and \(g(s, t)/(s\,t) = 0{,}6\,a\) for all \(s\) and \(t\), exactly the two mixed derivatives.

For a general function, though, the quotient \(g(s, t)/(s\,t)\) need not equal either of the mixed derivatives at \(P\). With the mean value theorem 1.84, used twice, we show that it equals a mixed derivative at some point inside the rectangle. For a function \(h\) of one variable that is continuous on the interval \([a, b]\) and has a derivative at every point between \(a\) and \(b\), the theorem says that the difference of the values at the end points equals the derivative at some intermediate point \(\xi\), multiplied by the length of the interval:

\[h(b) - h(a) = h'(\xi)\,(b - a) .\]

In figure 1.113 this is the chord and the tangent with the same slope at the point \(\xi\).

What happens when we shrink the rectangle? The point \(P\) is the lower left corner. The largest rectangle has the sides \(s\) and \(t\), and in it lies a point at which the mixed derivative equals \(g(s, t)/(s\,t)\). The rectangle half as large, with the sides \(s/2\) and \(t/2\), has its own such point, the one half as large again too. The drawn positions of the points are only an example, the mean value theorem says only that they lie in the rectangle. The point is at a distance from \(P\) of less than the diagonal of its rectangle, and this halves at every step. When the rectangle shrinks, the point therefore approaches \(P\), and if the mixed derivative is continuous, its value at the point approaches the value at \(P\).

Theorem 1.125 Symmetry of mixed partial derivatives (zamenljivost mešanih odvodov)

Let \(f\) be a function of three variables defined at all points whose distance from the point \(P = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) is less than some number \(r > 0\). Let the partial derivatives \(\partial f / \partial x\) and \(\partial f / \partial y\) and the mixed derivatives \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) and \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\) exist at all these points, and let the two mixed derivatives be continuous at the point \(P\) (definition 1.67). Then

\[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) . \tag{1.67}\]

The same holds for the variables \(x\) and \(z\) and for the variables \(y\) and \(z\).

Proof

We must show that the two mixed derivatives at \(P\) are the same number. Throughout the proof the coordinate \(z\) equals \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\), so we leave it out of the notation: \(f(x, y)\) means \(f(x, y, z_{\mathrm{P}})\), and likewise for the partial derivatives.

  1. We pick positive numbers \(s\) and \(t\) with \(s^2 + t^2 < r^2\). Every point \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + v, y_{\mathrm{P}} + w)\) with \(0 \le v \le s\) and \(0 \le w \le t\) is at the distance \(\sqrt{v^2 + w^2} \le \sqrt{s^2 + t^2} < r\) from \(P\) ((1.10)). So the rectangle with the corners \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \((x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t)\) lies entirely among the points at which, by assumption, we know all the derivatives used. Because the inequality \(\sqrt{s^2 + t^2} < r\) is strict, the points just outside the rectangle are also less than \(r\) from \(P\). So all the derivatives used exist on the edge of the rectangle too, as limits of difference quotients from both sides. Let \(g(s, t)\) be the double difference (1.66).
  2. For numbers \(v\) between \(0\) and \(t\) we define the function of one variable \(\varphi_1(v) = f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v)\). This is the change of \(f\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + v\). Putting in \(v = t\) and \(v = 0\) we get \(\varphi_1(t) - \varphi_1(0) = g(s, t)\), since these are exactly the four terms of (1.66). The value \(\varphi_1(t)\) is the change along the top side, and \(\varphi_1(0)\) the change along the bottom side.
  3. Each of the two terms of \(\varphi_1\) is the function \(f\) along a line in the direction of the axis \(y\). Its derivative with respect to \(v\) is, by the definition of the partial derivative 1.25, the partial derivative \(\partial f / \partial y\), which exists by assumption, and by step 1 at the end points \(v = 0\) and \(v = t\) too. The derivative of a difference is the difference of the derivatives (lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation), so at every point of the interval \([0, t]\)
    \[\varphi_1'(v) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v) .\]
    By lemma 1.79, that a differentiable function is continuous, \(\varphi_1\) is continuous on the interval \([0, t]\), at the end points too, as the mean value theorem in step 4 requires.
  4. By the mean value theorem 1.84 there is a number \(t_1\) between \(0\) and \(t\) such that \(\varphi_1(t) - \varphi_1(0) = \varphi_1'(t_1)\,t\). In the figure this is the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1\). By steps 2 and 3, therefore,
    \[g(s, t) = t\,\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1)\Big) .\]
  5. For numbers \(w\) between \(0\) and \(s\) we define \(\psi_1(w) = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1)\). The bracket of step 4 is \(\psi_1(s) - \psi_1(0)\). The function \(\psi_1\) is the function \(\partial f / \partial y\) along the horizontal segment at the height \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1\). Its derivative with respect to \(w\) is, by the definition of second partial derivatives 1.124, the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\), which exists by assumption, and by step 1 at the end points too. So \(\psi_1\) is differentiable at every point of the interval \([0, s]\). By lemma 1.79 it is therefore continuous on \([0, s]\).
  6. By the mean value theorem there is a number \(s_1\) between \(0\) and \(s\) such that \(\psi_1(s) - \psi_1(0) = \psi_1'(s_1)\,s\). Let \(Q_1 = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + s_1, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_1)\). With step 4 we get
    \[g(s, t) = s\,t\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1) .\]
  7. We proceed in the same way with the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) swapped. For numbers \(w\) between \(0\) and \(s\) let \(\varphi_2(w)\) be the change in the direction of the axis \(y\) at the place \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w\). For it, too, \(\varphi_2(s) - \varphi_2(0) = g(s, t)\), where \(\varphi_2(s)\) is the change along the right side and \(\varphi_2(0)\) the change along the left side. Let us also write the chain of steps 2 to 6 for this order, line by line:
    \[\begin{aligned} \varphi_2(w) &= f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t) - f(x_{\mathrm{P}} + w, y_{\mathrm{P}}) , && 0 \le w \le s , \\ g(s, t) &= \varphi_2(s) - \varphi_2(0) = s\,\varphi_2'(s_2) , \\ \psi_2(v) &= \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s_2, y_{\mathrm{P}} + v) , && 0 \le v \le t , \\ g(s, t) &= s\,\big(\psi_2(t) - \psi_2(0)\big) = s\,t\,\psi_2'(t_2) = s\,t\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) . \end{aligned}\]
    The first line corresponds to step 2. The second corresponds to step 4: the mean value theorem gives a number \(s_2\) between \(0\) and \(s\). The third corresponds to step 5, since \(\varphi_2'(s_2) = \psi_2(t) - \psi_2(0)\). The fourth corresponds to step 6: the theorem gives a number \(t_2\) between \(0\) and \(t\), and \(\psi_2'(t_2)\) is the mixed derivative first with respect to \(x\), then with respect to \(y\), at the point \(Q_2 = (x_{\mathrm{P}} + s_2, y_{\mathrm{P}} + t_2)\) on the vertical segment at \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + s_2\). The derivatives exist and the functions are continuous for the same reasons as in steps 3 and 5.
  8. The right-hand sides of steps 6 and 7 are equal, because both equal \(g(s, t)\). We divide them by \(s\,t \neq 0\) and get that the mixed derivative at \(Q_1\) equals the mixed derivative at \(Q_2\):
    \[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) .\]
  9. Now we use continuity. In figure 1.439 on the right, on the number line, \(m_1\) is the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\,(P)\) and \(m_2\) is the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\,(P)\), which we compare. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). Since \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\) is continuous at \(P\), for the error \(\eta/2\) there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that the value at every point whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(\delta_1\) differs from the value at \(P\) by less than \(\eta/2\) (the blue interval around \(m_1\)). Likewise, for \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\) there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\).
  10. Let \(\rho\) be the smallest of the numbers \(\delta_1\), \(\delta_2\) and \(r\), and take \(s = t = \rho/2\). In the figure there is the ball of radius \(\rho\) around \(P\), and in it the rectangle with the sides \(s\) and \(t\). Then \(s^2 + t^2 = \rho^2/2 < r^2\), so step 1 applies. The points \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are at a distance less than \(\sqrt{s^2 + t^2} = \rho/\sqrt 2 < \rho\) from \(P\), since their coordinates lie strictly between the coordinates of the corners. Therefore
    \[\Big|\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1)\Big| < \frac{\eta}{2} , \qquad \Big|\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P)\Big| < \frac{\eta}{2} .\]
  11. By step 8 the mixed derivatives at \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) have a common value \(c\), which by step 10 lies in both intervals. We write the difference of the values \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) by subtracting \(c\) and adding it again:
    \[m_1 - m_2 = (m_1 - c) + (c - m_2) .\]
    In the first bracket we put the value at \(Q_1\) for \(c\), in the second the value at \(Q_2\), since by step 8 both equal \(c\). The difference of the two mixed derivatives at \(P\) is thus the sum of the differences of step 10:
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P) &= \Big(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(P) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\,\partial y}(Q_1)\Big) \\ &\quad + \Big(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(Q_2) - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\,\partial x}(P)\Big) . \end{aligned}\]
    By the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\) (lemma 1.6, item 1), and by step 10 the absolute value of the left-hand side is less than \(\eta/2 + \eta/2 = \eta\).
  12. We picked the error \(\eta\) freely. The absolute value of the difference of the two mixed derivatives at \(P\) is not negative and is smaller than every positive number, so by lemma 1.34 on an inequality tested with all positive numbers it equals zero. The mixed derivatives at \(P\) are equal.
  13. For the variables \(x\) and \(z\) and for \(y\) and \(z\) steps 1 to 12 are the same, only with the variables renamed.

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 8.6.2 (PDF pp. 60-62). The source assumes that all partial derivatives up to second order are continuous at all points of an open set, and remarks that continuity of the two mixed derivatives is enough. The proof uses continuity only at the point \(P\). Steps 9 to 12 replace the limit of a function of two variables used by the source and are not from the source.

The proof wrote the double difference twice as the product of \(s\,t\) and a mixed derivative, once with one order of differentiation and once with the other, each time at some point inside the rectangle. As the rectangle shrinks, both points approach \(P\), and the continuity of the mixed derivatives makes their values approach the values at \(P\). The mean value theorem did the same job here, twice, as for the change of a field over a short step in section 1.15: it turned a difference of values into a derivative at a point in between.

Is the assumption of continuity needed? It is. In Exercise 8.6.2 (PDF p. 62), LEBL2 gives the function of two variables

\[f(x, y) = \frac{x\,y\,(x^2 - y^2)}{x^2 + y^2} \quad \text{for } (x, y) \neq (0, 0) , \qquad f(0, 0) = 0 ,\]

whose first order partial derivatives exist and are continuous, while the mixed derivatives exist but are not continuous at the origin and differ there (figure 1.440).

What does the surface \(f\) look like? The denominator \(x^2 + y^2\) is positive, so \(f\) has the sign of the numerator \(x\,y\,(x^2 - y^2)\). Let us draw it. The axes are \(x\) and \(y\). On them \(f\) is zero, because \(x\,y = 0\) there. The grey dashed diagonals are the lines \(y = x\) and \(y = -x\), where \(x^2 = y^2\), so \(f\) is zero on them too. The axes and the diagonals divide the plane into eight angles. Plus stands in the angles where \(f\) is positive, for example at \(x > y > 0\), where \(x\,y\) and \(x^2 - y^2\) are positive. Minus stands in the angles where \(f\) is negative, for example at \(y > x > 0\). The surface is thus alternately above the plane and below it, eight times on one turn around the origin. The blue arrow from the point \((0, 1)\) points in the direction of the axis \(x\), into an angle with a minus: \(f\) decreases there with \(x\), so \(\partial f / \partial x\,(0, 1)\) is negative. The blue arrow from the point \((1, 0)\) points in the direction of the axis \(y\), into an angle with a plus: \(f\) increases there with \(y\), so \(\partial f / \partial y\,(1, 0)\) is positive. Let us compute these two derivatives exactly.

On the axis \(y\) the difference quotient with respect to \(x\) is \(\big(f(h, y) - f(0, y)\big)/h = y\,(h^2 - y^2)/(h^2 + y^2)\), and as \(h\) goes to zero with \(y \neq 0\), the numerator approaches \(-y^3\), the denominator \(y^2\), and the quotient \(-y\). So \(\partial f / \partial x\,(0, y) = -y\), and this holds at \(y = 0\) too, since \(f\) is zero everywhere on the axis \(x\). In the same way we get the value \(\partial f / \partial y\,(x, 0) = x\) on the axis \(x\). Therefore \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\,(0, 0) = -1\), \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\,(0, 0) = 1\) (figure 1.441). That the two are not both continuous at the origin is already told by the theorem: if both were continuous, they would be equal by the theorem, but they are \(-1\) and \(1\). The source adds that neither of them is continuous at the origin. For the hanging bar and for the strips of this section the displacement components are polynomials. Their partial derivatives of all orders are polynomials again, and these are continuous everywhere by corollary 1.69, that polynomials in \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are continuous.

Let us draw these two first derivatives. On the left graph the blue line is the derivative \(\partial f / \partial x\,(0, y)\) as a function of \(y\), which equals \(-y\). The slope of the line is \(-1\): for a step \(h\) to the right the value changes by \(-h\). This is the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial y\,\partial x\,(0, 0) = -1\). On the right graph the blue line is the derivative \(\partial f / \partial y\,(x, 0)\) as a function of \(x\), which equals \(x\). Its slope is \(1\), and this is the mixed derivative \(\partial^2 f / \partial x\,\partial y\,(0, 0) = 1\). The lines slope in opposite directions, so the mixed derivatives at the origin are not equal.

In the equations we are looking for we will differentiate three times and swap the order in several places. So we extend the theorem to third derivatives. We draw the six orders \(a\,b\,c\) as a hexagon (figure 1.442). Each corner is one order of differentiation, we start at \(a\,b\,c\) at the top. In the middle is written what the corner \(a\,b\,c\) means: the third derivative \(\partial^3 f / \partial a\,\partial b\,\partial c\), which we read from right to left, first with respect to \(c\), then to \(b\), last to \(a\). Each side is one swap of two neighbouring letters. The blue sides swap the first two letters, the outer pair next to the blue bracket in the middle, which are the last two differentiations. The blackwhite ones swap the last two letters, the inner pair next to the blackwhite bracket, which are the first two differentiations. Blue and blackwhite alternate, because the same swap twice in a row would bring back the previous order. By alternating we go around all six orders and after six swaps we come to \(a\,b\,c\) again.

Corollary 1.126 Independence of the order of differentiation (neodvisnost od vrstnega reda odvajanja)

Let \(D\) be a set of points in which every point is interior, that is, around every point \(P\) of \(D\) there is a number \(r > 0\) such that all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\) are in \(D\). Let a function \(f\) have partial derivatives of first, second and third order at every point of \(D\), and let all these derivatives be continuous at every point of \(D\). Then at every point of \(D\) the second and third partial derivatives of \(f\) do not depend on the order in which we differentiate.

Proof

We must show that for second and third partial derivatives a swap of the order of differentiation does not change the value. Let \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) be variables, each of them \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\).

1. Second derivatives.

  1. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\) and \(r\) its number from the assumption. The function \(f\) is defined at all points whose distance from \(P\) is less than \(r\), its first and second partial derivatives exist there, and the mixed derivatives are continuous at \(P\). By theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives (figure 1.439, the values \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are equal), \(\partial^2 f / \partial a\,\partial b\,(P) = \partial^2 f / \partial b\,\partial a\,(P)\).

2. Third derivatives.

  1. Swapping the inner pair. By the first part, the functions \(\partial^2 f / \partial b\,\partial c\) and \(\partial^2 f / \partial c\,\partial b\) are equal at every point of \(D\). Equal functions have equal difference quotients and so equal partial derivatives, therefore \(\partial^3 f / \partial a\,\partial b\,\partial c = \partial^3 f / \partial a\,\partial c\,\partial b\) at every point of \(D\).
  2. Swapping the outer pair. Let \(h = \partial f / \partial c\). Its first partial derivatives are second partial derivatives of \(f\), and its second partial derivatives are third partial derivatives of \(f\), which exist and are continuous. By theorem 1.125 applied to \(h\), \(\partial^2 h / \partial a\,\partial b = \partial^2 h / \partial b\,\partial a\), that is, \(\partial^3 f / \partial a\,\partial b\,\partial c = \partial^3 f / \partial b\,\partial a\,\partial c\) at every point of \(D\).
  3. From the order \(a\,b\,c\) we get all six orders by a chain of swaps, each time swapping either the outer or the inner pair:
    \[a\,b\,c \to b\,a\,c \to b\,c\,a \to c\,b\,a \to c\,a\,b \to a\,c\,b .\]
    By steps 1 and 2 no swap changes the value, so all orders are equivalent. If two of the variables are equal, there are fewer different orders, but the chain still covers them all.

Source: LEBL2 Exercise 8.6.3 (PDF p. 62) states the claim for derivatives of any order. The proof is not from the source.

A function whose partial derivatives up to third order exist and are continuous at every point of a set is called by LEBL2 a three times continuously differentiable function (LEBL2 Def. 8.6.1, PDF p. 60). For a displacement field this is more than the continuous differentiability of definition 1.90 requires. The body has no cracks, and the strains and their first and second partial derivatives change from point to point without jumps. We will need this assumption for the equations we are looking for. It fails, for example, at a crack or at a point where a force concentrated at one point acts on the body (section 1.15).

1.18.3 Compatibility equations

Let us return to the strip of section 1.18.1. A thin steel strip of length 200 mm and height 20 mm lies in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), the axis \(x\) along the strip, the origin at the middle of the left end. We prescribed the strains (1.64) to it, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), with \(k = -10\) m⁻². Let us show that there is no displacement field with these strains. Let us first draw the idea (figure 1.443). On the left, the grey dashed lines are two longitudinal fibres before the deformation, the lower at the height \(y = 0\) and the upper at \(y = 5\) mm, straight, because the strip is still straight. The arrows between the halves show the directions of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), which hold for both halves: the fibres lie in the direction of the axis \(x\), the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) is vertical. The orange curves are the fibres after the deformation. Everything is greatly magnified. The curves are equal, only shifted. This is what \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) demands: the transverse fibres keep their length, so the points of both fibres at the same \(x\) move equally in the direction of the axis \(y\) (step 1 below). The blue dimensions stand on the same vertical line, that is, at the same value of \(x\), and show the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) of each fibre. They are equally long. On the right the dashed lines are again the fibres before the deformation. The lower orange line is the fibre at \(y = 0\), as the strains demand it: straight, so the label beside it has the second derivative zero. The upper orange curve is the fibre at \(y = 5\) mm, curved, with the second derivative \(-2k\,y\), which we derive in steps 3 to 6 and which at \(y = 5\) mm equals \(0{,}1\ \text{m}^{-1}\) (step 7). We took the height 5 mm because one of the five fibres that we drew at the start lies there. Every height except zero would give the same conclusion. Both curves start with the same slope, so that the difference is only in the curvature. The two pictures contradict each other: the left demands the same shape for both fibres, the right two different curvatures. So there is no displacement field. Let us also write the idea in two lines:

  • the transverse fibres keep their length (\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\)), so both fibres bend into the same shape \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x)\) (steps 1 and 2 below),
  • without shear (\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\)), however, the fibre at the height \(y\) must curve, as we saw on the piece with right angles and on the row of pieces, the more the faster \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) changes with height, exactly so that \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = -\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y = -2k\,y\), that is \(0\) at \(y = 0\) and \(0{,}1\ \text{m}^{-1}\) at \(y = 5\) mm (steps 3 to 6).

The same shape cannot have two different second derivatives. The bands at these heights therefore curve differently, as in figure 1.431, right. We argue by contradiction: suppose that at the interior points of the strip there is a displacement field whose components have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order and which gives these strains.

  1. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = 0\) at every point, \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) has derivative zero along every transverse segment on which \(x\) and \(z\) are constant. By corollary 1.85 on a function with zero derivative, applied on the interval between \(0\) and \(y\), we have \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) = u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 0, z)\) for every \(y\). All points of a transverse segment move equally in the direction of the axis \(y\).
  2. So \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) and \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2\) do not depend on \(y\) either, both fibres have the same shape. Indeed, at the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, 0, z)\) the difference quotients with respect to \(x\) are equal, because the values are equal, and so their limits are equal too.
  3. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), by (1.63) \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0\), that is, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = -\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) at every point. The right angle between a longitudinal and a transverse fibre stays right, so the longitudinal fibre turns by the same angle and in the same direction as the transverse fibre, as on piece (2) of figure 1.432. The minus is in the equation because \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) measures the rise of the longitudinal fibre and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) the shift of the transverse fibre to the right. In a counterclockwise turn, as on piece (2), the longitudinal fibre rises and the transverse one shifts to the left.
  4. Equal functions have equal partial derivatives with respect to \(x\): \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = -\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\,\partial y\).
  5. By theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives, \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\,\partial y = \partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\,\partial x = \partial / \partial y\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x) = \partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\).
  6. For the prescribed strain \(\partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y = \partial(k\,y^2)/\partial y = 2k\,y\) (lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation). With steps 4 and 5, the second derivative of the fibre at the height \(y\) is
    \[\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x^2} = -2k\,y .\]
  7. By step 2 the left-hand side does not depend on \(y\), but the right-hand side does. At \(y = 0\) the right-hand side is \(0\), at \(y = 5\) mm it is \(-2 \cdot (-10\ \text{m}^{-2}) \cdot 0{,}005\ \text{m} = 0{,}1\ \text{m}^{-1}\). This is a contradiction, so there is no displacement field with the prescribed strains.

The computation also tells us why the bands in figure 1.431 curve. The partial derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) is the slope of a longitudinal fibre after straining: how much the fibre rises per unit length. The second derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2\) says how fast this slope changes along the fibre. A fibre that has the same slope everywhere is straight. The faster the slope changes, the more strongly the fibre is curved. Steps 3 to 6 say that in a strip without shear \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = -\partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\): the longitudinal fibre at the height \(y\) curves the more strongly, the faster the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) changes with height there. Steps 1 and 2 say that when the transverse fibres keep their length, all longitudinal fibres curve equally. Both requirements can hold together only if \(\partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\) is the same at all heights. For \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\) we have \(\partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y = 1/R\) everywhere, and indeed \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = \partial^2(-x^2/(2R))/\partial x^2 = -1/R\). For \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), though, \(2k\,y\) differs at different heights.

We drew the same with pieces in figure 1.432 in section 1.18.1. On piece (1) the right edge tilts by \(-\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y + \Delta y) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y)\big)\,\Delta x / \Delta y\) horizontal distances per unit height. On piece (2) the slope of the longitudinal fibre changes over the length \(\Delta x\) by about as much, so per unit length by \(-\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y + \Delta y) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(y)\big)/\Delta y\). When we shorten \(\Delta x\), the change of slope per unit length approaches \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2\), and when we shorten \(\Delta y\), the quotient approaches \(-\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\). So the figure shows where the equality \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = -\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\) from steps 3 to 6 comes from, which the proof states exactly.

What if the transverse fibres do not keep their length, or the right angles change? Then step 1 or 3 of the proof no longer holds, and the longitudinal fibres at different heights can curve differently. Let us take the first possibility. For the first strip we keep \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), but we do not prescribe the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\). We look for the displacement field in the same way as for the second strip, with the equations for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so that the right angles stay right:

\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} = k\,y^2 , \qquad \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} = 0 .\]
  1. The function \(k\,x\,y^2\) has the derivative \(k\,y^2\) with respect to \(x\), since \(k\,y^2\) is a constant number here. Let us take \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2\), and the first equation holds.
  2. The derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(y\) is \(2k\,x\,y\), so by the second equation \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = -2k\,x\,y\). The function \(-k\,x^2\,y\) has such a derivative with respect to \(x\), so let us take \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y\).
  3. This \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) depends on \(y\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is not zero, but \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y = -k\,x^2\).

The field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) therefore gives the strains

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0 .\]

Let us call this strip the corrected strip. It has the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) of the first strip, but the transverse fibres lengthen by \(-k\,x^2\), which is positive, because \(k\) is negative, and grows toward the right end of the strip. So step 1 of the proof above does not hold here.

Let us draw this strip. The grey dashed rectangle with five horizontal lines is the strip before the deformation, with five longitudinal fibres. It is drawn in the units of the figure: the heights of the fibres run from \(-1\) to \(1\), the length of the strip is \(4\). The arrows show the directions of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), the origin is at the middle of the left end. So that the deformation can be seen, we took \(k = -0{,}05\) per square unit of the figure. The orange curves are the fibres after the deformation. The middle fibre stays straight, the others curve, the more the farther from the middle they are, and each differently. The thick orange curve on the right is the right transverse fibre after the deformation. At \(x = 4\) we have \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}05 \cdot 16 = 0{,}8\), so it is almost twice as long as the original. The longitudinal fibre at the height \(y\) has the shape \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,x^2\,y\), which depends on \(y\), with the second derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x^2 = -2k\,y\). This is exactly the second derivative that step 6 requires, and the fibres at different heights curve differently.

With \(k = -10\) m⁻², however, this example is no longer one of small strains. At the right end of the strip, at \(x = 200\) mm,

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,(0{,}2\ \text{m})^2 = \begin{cases} 0{,}4 , & k = -10\ \text{m}^{-2} , \\ 0{,}001 , & k = -0{,}025\ \text{m}^{-2} . \end{cases}\]

The first value is \(400\) times the bound \(0{,}001\) that the small deformation assumption sets for steel structures (section 1.17.3), and there the small strain tensor no longer tells accurately how much the fibres lengthen. With \(k = -0{,}025\) m⁻², however, the largest \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is exactly \(0{,}001\), while \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) at the edges is only \(2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-6}\). All computations of this section are linear in \(k\): at another \(k\) the strains, the displacements and all their derivatives are only multiplied by the same number. So everything that follows holds at every \(k\), and we kept the letter \(k\) so that the strip can be compared with the first one. The general condition, which says how much the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and the shear \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) must make up for fibres at different heights curving differently, is the first of the six equations in the following theorem.

From history

Let us draw a timeline. The axis shows years. The relations given by the theorem below were first obtained by Saint-Venant in 1864, without using rotations (the small rotation tensor of definition 1.116). The proof that he indicated was developed later by Gustav Robert Kirchhoff, and the proof through rotations is the work of Eugenio Beltrami, published in 1889 (LOVE, PDF pp. 68-69).

Let us return to the strains of the strip. The following theorem gives the six equations that the strain components, calculated from the displacement field, satisfy. The first of them is the condition that the first strip does not satisfy. To the right of each equation is written the plane or axis that it belongs to, and we explain this in the proof.

Theorem 1.127 Compatibility equations (enačbe kompatibilnosti)

Let \(D\) be a set of points in which every point is interior, and let the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) of a displacement field have, at every point of \(D\), partial derivatives of first, second and third order that are continuous at every point of \(D\). Then the strain components (1.63) satisfy, at every point of \(D\), the equations

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} &= 2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} , && (1)\ \ \text{plane } x\text{-}y \\ \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial z^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial y^2} &= 2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} , && (2)\ \ \text{plane } y\text{-}z \\ \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial z^2} &= 2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} , && (3)\ \ \text{plane } z\text{-}x \\[3mm] \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x^2} &= \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} , && (4)\ \ \text{os } x \\ \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial y^2} &= \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} , && (5)\ \ \text{os } y \\ \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial z^2} &= \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} . && (6)\ \ \text{os } z \end{aligned} \tag{1.68}\]
Proof

We must show that each of the six equations holds when we put the components (1.63) into it. The strain components are first partial derivatives of the displacements or halves of their sums, so their second partial derivatives are third partial derivatives of the displacements. By corollary 1.126 on the independence of the order of differentiation, the third partial derivatives of the displacements do not depend on the order of differentiation. We compute partial derivatives as ordinary derivatives, so the two rules of lemma 1.81 hold for them: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant factor can be taken out.

We shorten the proof with the pattern that the equations have. Let us draw it. The three corners of the triangle are the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The numbers beside the sides are equations (1) to (3). The side between two corners is the plane of these two axes, as written beside the equation in the theorem: the side between \(x\) and \(y\) carries equation (1). The numbers beside the corners are equations (4) to (6), the corner \(x\) carries equation (4). The blue arrows beside the sides show the renaming of the axes \(x \to y \to z \to x\) and close into a circle. In the renaming each side goes to the next one, so equation (1) goes to (2), and this at the next renaming to (3). Each corner goes to the next one, so (4) goes to (5), and this to (6). The proof therefore derives only equations (1) and (4), and gets the other four by renaming. In the theorem we read the pattern as follows:

  • equations (1) to (3), one for each of the planes \(x\)-\(y\), \(y\)-\(z\) and \(z\)-\(x\), contain the second derivative of each of the two normal strains in the directions of this plane and the second derivative of the shear in it,
  • equations (4) to (6), one for each of the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), contain the second derivative of the normal strain in the direction of this axis and the second derivatives of the shears in all three planes.

1. The first equation.

The goal is to write the left-hand side as a second derivative of the sum \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\), which by (1.63) equals \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). So in each term we put one derivative with respect to \(x\) and one with respect to \(y\) in front of the bracket.

  1. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\), \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2\) is a third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), once with respect to \(x\) and twice with respect to \(y\). By the same corollary we can write it as
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\Big) .\]
  2. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\), \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x^2\) is a third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), once with respect to \(y\) and twice with respect to \(x\). By the same corollary,
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) .\]
  3. We add the equalities of steps 1 and 2. The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, so
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) .\]
  4. By (1.63) the sum in the bracket is \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). We take out the constant factor \(2\) and get the first equation of (1.68).

2. The second and third equations.

  1. We rename the axes: \(x\) to \(y\), \(y\) to \(z\) and \(z\) to \(x\). The components of the strain are renamed as follows:
    \[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} &\to \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} . \end{aligned}\]
