    The equations (1.63) then turn into each other. From \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\) we get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\), from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) we get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\), and from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) we get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\), which by definition equals \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The assumption of the theorem does not change either. So the steps of the first part hold with the renamed axes, and the first equation becomes
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial z^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}}{\partial y^2} = 2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} ,\]
    which is the second equation.
  2. When we rename the axes once more in the same way, the second equation becomes the third. In it \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) appears, and by corollary 1.126 on the independence of the order of differentiation the order of differentiation in \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} / \partial z\,\partial x\) does not matter.

3. The fourth equation. We write each term with the displacements by (1.63) and look at which third derivatives of the displacements it contains.

  1. The first term of the left-hand side is a third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), with respect to \(x\), to \(y\) and to \(z\):
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y\,\partial z} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial y\,\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}\Big) .\]
  2. The second term of the left-hand side is
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}}{\partial x^2} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z}\Big) + \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\Big) ,\]
    half the third derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), twice by \(x\) and once by \(z\), plus half that of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\), twice by \(x\) and once by \(y\).
  3. The first term of the right-hand side is
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}\Big) + \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial y}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) ,\]
    half of the third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and half of the third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(y\).
  4. The second term of the right-hand side is
    \[\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial z} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\Big) + \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x\,\partial z}\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) ,\]
    half of the third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and half of the third partial derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(z\).
  5. By corollary 1.126 on the independence of the order of differentiation, third derivatives of the same component with respect to the same variables are equal, whatever the order. On the right-hand side the two halves of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) therefore add up to the whole derivative, which equals the first term on the left from step 1. The half of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) from step 3 equals the second half from step 2, and the half of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) from step 4 equals the first half from step 2. So the right-hand side equals the left-hand side, and the fourth equation holds.

Let us draw steps 1 to 5 in one place. Three different third derivatives of the displacements appear in the terms. The figure has a pair of columns for each, and the label above the pair writes it: the first pair for the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) with respect to \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), the second for the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(z\) and the third for the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) twice with respect to \(x\) and once with respect to \(y\). The left column of a pair is the left-hand side of the equation, the right column the right-hand side, and between them is the sign \(=\). The height of a section in a column is the factor with which the term contains this derivative, a whole derivative is 1 high. Each term has its own colour, as the legend under the columns tells. The first term of the left side is blue and by step 1 contains the whole derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\). The second term of the left side is grey and by step 2 contains half of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and half of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\). The first term of the right side is orange and by step 3 contains half of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and half of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\). The second term of the right side is blackwhite and by step 4 contains half of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and half of the derivative of \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\). In each pair the columns are equally high, \(1 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\), \(\tfrac12 = \tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac12 = \tfrac12\), and this is step 5.

4. The fifth and sixth equations.

  1. When we rename the axes in the fourth equation as in the second part, \(x\) to \(y\), \(y\) to \(z\) and \(z\) to \(x\), and use \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and the fact that the order of differentiation does not matter, we get the fifth equation. One more renaming gives the sixth.

Source: CM (3.7.4)-(3.7.9) (PDF pp. 150-151), SADD (2.6.2) (PDF p. 51), BARBER (2.8)-(2.9) (PDF p. 45). CM derives the first equation and only states the others, SADD derives them in index notation.

The equations (1.68) are called the Saint-Venant compatibility equations (CM, PDF p. 149, SADD, PDF p. 51). The proof showed where they come from: the strain components are derivatives of only three functions, and when we differentiate them twice more, the same third derivatives of the displacements appear in several places. The equations are exactly these repetitions, written without the displacements.

Let us test the equations on three strips. For the strip with the strains (1.64), \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2 = \partial(2k\,y)/\partial y = 2k\), while the other two terms of the first equation are zero, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are zero. The first equation would require \(2k + 0 = 0\), but for \(k = -10\) m⁻² the left-hand side is \(-20\) m⁻². The equation fails, so by the theorem no displacement field with continuous derivatives up to third order gives these strains, as we already showed above. For the strip with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = y/R\), on the other hand, \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2 = 0\), and the first equation holds, \(0 + 0 = 0\). For the corrected strip with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -k\,x^2\) we have \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x^2 = -2k\), and the first equation holds, \(2k - 2k = 0\). The other five equations hold for all three strips, because no component depends on \(z\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero. All three strips at a glance:

strip \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) left side of the first equation right side displacement field
first \(k\,y^2\) \(0\) \(0\) \(2k\) \(0\) none
second \(y/R\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \((x\,y/R,\ -x^2/(2R),\ 0)\)
corrected \(k\,y^2\) \(-k\,x^2\) \(0\) \(2k - 2k = 0\) \(0\) \((k\,x\,y^2,\ -k\,x^2\,y,\ 0)\)

What does the first equation say? Let us write it once more and put under the terms the letters with which we will name them:

\[\underbrace{\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2}}_{(\mathrm{a})} + \underbrace{\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2}}_{(\mathrm{b})} = \underbrace{2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y}}_{(\mathrm{c})} .\]

For each term let us write what it measures.

  • (a) By steps 3 to 6 of the proof and by the row of pieces in figure 1.432, \(-\partial \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y\) is how strongly a longitudinal fibre curves when there is no shear. The term (a) says how fast this curving changes with the height \(y\). For the first strip it is \(2k\) and not zero, so the fibres at different heights curve differently.
  • (b) The same for the transverse fibres, with the roles of the axes swapped: how fast the curving of the transverse fibres changes with \(x\) when there is no shear. For the corrected strip it is \(-2k\) and cancels the term (a).
  • (c) The shear term: how the change of the right angles, the shear \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), changes with \(x\) and \(y\) together. The example below shows that it can cancel the term (a) as well, with the right angles changing.

The equation therefore says that the sum of the terms (a) and (b) equals the term (c): how much the curvings of the longitudinal and transverse fibres at different places fail to agree must be made up exactly by the change of the right angles, otherwise the pieces do not fit together.

An example: for the first strip we correct the right angles instead of the transverse fibres. The strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = k\,x\,y\) come from the field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = k\,x\,y^2\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), since \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x = k\,y^2\) and \(\tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x) = \tfrac12 \cdot 2k\,x\,y\). Let us draw the strip. The grey dashed grid is the strip before the deformation, with five longitudinal and five transverse fibres. It is drawn in the units of the figure: it runs from \(y = -1\) to \(1\) and from \(x = 0\) to \(4\), the arrows show the directions of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), and \(k = -0{,}12\) per square unit of the figure. The fifth transverse fibre is the left edge, \(x = 0\), which stays in place, because \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) there. The deformation is greatly magnified. In orange are the fibres after the deformation. The longitudinal fibres do not curve at all here, because \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). Instead four transverse fibres curve. Each is a parabola, because a point at the height \(y\) moves horizontally by \(k\,x\,y^2\), the more the farther from the middle it is. So the right angles change. At \(x = 3\) and \(y = \pm 1\) the grey tangents of the transverse fibre are drawn, both directed upward, in the direction of increasing \(y\). The grey arcs measure the angle from the direction of the axis \(x\) to these tangents. At the top the tangent points out of the strip, so the arc is above the strip, at the bottom it points into the strip.

Before the deformation this angle is a right angle. Let us compute it after the deformation. The point of the transverse fibre that was at \((x, y)\) is at \((x + k\,x\,y^2,\ y)\) after the deformation. When we move up along the fibre, its coordinate \(x\) changes with the derivative \(2k\,x\,y\) with respect to \(y\), and the coordinate \(y\) with the derivative \(1\), so the tangent has the direction \((2k\,x\,y,\ 1)\). At \(x = 3\), \(y = \pm 1\) and \(k = -0{,}12\)

\[(2k\,x\,y,\ 1) = \big(2 \cdot (-0{,}12) \cdot 3 \cdot (\pm 1),\ 1\big) = (\mp 0{,}72,\ 1) .\]

At the top the tangent is tilted to the left of the vertical by an angle whose tangent is \(0{,}72\), that is \(35{,}8^\circ\), so the angle from the axis \(x\) to it is \(90^\circ + 35{,}8^\circ = 125{,}8^\circ\). At the bottom it is tilted by the same angle to the right, and the angle is \(90^\circ - 35{,}8^\circ = 54{,}2^\circ\). The first equation holds: the left side is \(2k + 0\), the right side \(2\,\partial^2(k\,x\,y)/\partial x\,\partial y = 2k\). The factor \(2\) is on the right because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is only half of the sum \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\). The shear has thus corrected the mismatch of the first strip: there the left side \(2k\) stayed without a partner, here the right side cancels it. The first strip can therefore be corrected in two ways, by lengthening the transverse fibres, as in the corrected strip (term (b)), or by changing the right angles, as here (term (c)). The left side must equal the right side, otherwise the pieces do not fit together.

For the hanging bar the test is short. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, the axis \(x\) pointing down from the centre \(O\) of the top end. By (1.63) and the table of partial derivatives in section 1.7.2 its strains are

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2a\,(L - x) , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 .\]

Let us draw the strains over the depth. The axes are the depth \(x\) and the strain. The blue line is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2a\,(L - x)\), which falls from the value \(2aL\) at the top to zero at \(x = L\). Below the cross-section at \(x = L\) nothing hangs that would pull it, since the pull in the bar falls from the weight of the whole bar at the top to zero at the lower end (section 1.2). Without a pull the material does not stretch there. The blackwhite line is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\), with the value \(-0{,}6\,aL\) at the top. It lies below the axis, because the bar is contracted in the transverse direction, and it rises to zero at \(x = L\). The slope of a line is its derivative. For both it is constant, \(-2a\) for the blue one and \(0{,}6\,a\) for the blackwhite one.

The shear strains are zero because the pairs of partial derivatives off the diagonal of the table cancel, for example \(\tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y + 0{,}6\,a\,y) = 0\). In the first equation \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2\) and \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x^2\) are zero. The first is zero because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) does not depend on \(y\). The second is zero because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is a straight line in \(x\) with the derivative \(0{,}6\,a\), which is constant and has derivative zero. The right-hand side is zero because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is zero. The equation holds, \(0 + 0 = 0\). In the same way, in all the other equations all second derivatives of the strains are zero, because the strains depend only on \(x\), and at most linearly. It must be so, since we got the strains from a displacement field whose components are polynomials and so have continuous derivatives of all orders. The check is short because the strains of the bar are straight lines, linear functions of the coordinates, and second derivatives of linear functions are zero. Every strain field that is a linear function of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) therefore satisfies all six equations. The equations check something only for strains that change nonlinearly with the coordinates, as in the strips above.

A few remarks on the equations.

  1. In plane problems, where \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) depend only on \(x\) and \(y\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero and no strain depends on \(z\). Only the first equation remains, and the other five turn into \(0 = 0\) (BARBER, PDF p. 45).
  2. Books that use the engineering shear strain \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) write the first equation as \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2 + \partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x^2 = \partial^2 \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} / \partial x\,\partial y\), without the factor \(2\). CM writes the components \(\varepsilon_{11}\), \(\varepsilon_{12}\) and the coordinates \(X_1\), \(X_2\), SADD writes \(e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(e_{\mathrm{xy}}\), both with half the shear as we do.
  3. We might expect three equations, since six functions come from three, \(6 - 3 = 3\). In the plane counting works: the three functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) come from two, \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\), and one equation remains, the first (remark 1). In space, though, there are six equations, and none of them can be derived from the other five (BARBER, PDF p. 45). We see the reason in (1.68): every equation contains second derivatives that appear in no other one, the first for example \(\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} / \partial y^2\). For each equation we can therefore find strains that satisfy the other five but not it. For the first these are the strains of the first strip, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), with the others zero. So none of the six equations may be left out. SADD (PDF p. 51), however, says that the six equations are not independent, because there are relations among them involving derivatives, and that they can be reduced to three independent equations of fourth order. This does not contradict BARBER, since the relations are among the derivatives of the equations, not among the equations themselves. We denote by \(R_1, \dots, R_6\) the left side of each of the six equations minus its right side. For any six functions with continuous partial derivatives up to the third order,
    \[\frac{\partial R_2}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial R_6}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R_5}{\partial z} .\]
    When we insert \(R_2\), \(R_5\) and \(R_6\), on the right the terms with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the terms with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) cancel, and the other three terms equal the three terms on the left by corollary 1.126. Two similar relations follow by renaming the axes. If the fifth and sixth equations hold, the relation gives only \(\partial R_2 / \partial x = 0\): \(R_2\) does not change in the direction of the axis \(x\), but it need not be zero. The second equation does not follow from the fifth and sixth, but its derivative with respect to \(x\) does. Conclusions from counting equations with numbers for equations with derivatives therefore do not always hold (BARBER, PDF p. 45).
  4. The equations hold for the small strain tensor. For the Green-Lagrange strain tensor (definition 1.112) there are conditions for fitting together too. CM writes them with the deformation gradient, while the form with the Green-Lagrange tensor is so involved that it does not derive it (CM, PDF pp. 149 and 154).
  5. We need the equations only when we solve a problem with strains or with forces in the material, not with displacements. When we first find the displacements and compute the strains from them, the strains fit together by themselves (CM, PDF p. 154, SADD, PDF p. 54). We will use them in chapter 11.

1.18.4 A field without strain

Theorem 1.127 gave a condition that the strains satisfy when they come from a displacement field. Before we ask whether the condition is also enough, let us answer another question. Suppose that a displacement field with the given strains exists. Is it the only one? Let us write the question on the board, and above it the answer that we already know for the bar from section 1.14.6 (corollary 1.85 on a function with zero derivative). Two displacements of the bar \(u\) and \(\tilde u\) have the same strain when they have the same derivative:

\[\begin{aligned} &\text{bar:} && \tilde u'(x) = u'(x) \text{ for every } x \\ &&&\Longrightarrow\quad \tilde u(x) = u(x) + c , \ c \text{ the same number for all } x , \\ &\text{body:} && \text{fields } \tilde{\vek u} \text{ and } \vek u \text{ have at every point the same } \ten\varepsilon \\ &&&\Longrightarrow\quad \tilde{\vek u}(P) = \vek u(P) + \ ? \end{aligned}\]

For the bar the added term \(c\) is the same shift of all points. In space we expect more freedom. We can shift a body as a whole and also turn it, without changing the distance between any two of its points (section 1.6), like the square plate of section 1.17.6. Such an exact rigid-body displacement changes the length of no fibre: the fibre \(OA\) is \(5\) long before the rotation and after it. May we add it to every displacement field without changing the small strain tensor? We will see that not quite, and that the right term is a field that is a rigid-body displacement only to first order.

For an exact rotation that keeps all distances, though, the small strain tensor shows a strain that is not there, even when the rotation is small. In section 1.17.6 we turned a square plate about the axis \(z\) with the numbers \(s = 0{,}001\) and \(c = \sqrt{1 - s^2}\) and got \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c - 1 = -5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), although the plate was not strained. An exact rotation would therefore change the small strain tensor of the field to which we add it by \(-5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\). Which displacements have a small strain tensor of exactly zero? In section 1.17.5 we stated that a displacement given by an antisymmetric matrix that is the same at all points is a rigid rotation when the entries of the matrix are small (CM, PDF p. 143). Let us add to it a shift of all points by the same vector. We get the field

\[\vek u(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} ,\]

where \(\vek a\) is a constant vector, \(\mat W\) a constant antisymmetric matrix (definition 1.102), and \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = \overrightarrow{OP} = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) the vector from the origin \(O\) to the point \(P\), whose components are the coordinates of \(P\). The component \(\ix{i}\) of the displacement is \(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = a_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\), where as before \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\) and \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). The partial derivative of this component with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \(W_{\mathrm{ij}}\): the number \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant, the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) has the derivative \(1\) with respect to itself, and the other two coordinates are constant in this differentiation (lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation). For the component \(x\) and the derivative with respect to \(y\) this is

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = a_{\mathrm{x}} + W_{\mathrm{xx}}\,x + W_{\mathrm{xy}}\,y + W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,z , \qquad \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} = 0 + 0 + W_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot 1 + 0 = W_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]

The displacement gradient is therefore \(\mat W\) at every point, and the small strain tensor is \(\tfrac12(\mat W + \mat W^\T) = \tfrac12(\mat W - \mat W) = \mat 0\). The small rotation tensor is \(\tfrac12(\mat W - \mat W^\T) = \mat W\). An example is a rotation about the axis \(z\), for which the matrix has a single pair of nonzero entries:

\[\mat W = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -s & 0 \\ s & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = (-s\,y_{\mathrm{P}},\ s\,x_{\mathrm{P}},\ 0) .\]

Let us draw this, seen from above, along the axis \(z\). On the left the blackwhite square is the plate before the movement, with the corner \(O\) at the origin. Its opposite corner is the point \(P\). The grey dashed line from \(O\) to \(P\) is the vector \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\). The rotation is greatly magnified: instead of \(s = 0{,}001\), \(s = 0{,}3\) is drawn, so that it can be seen. The point \(P\) moves perpendicular to the vector \((x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, 0)\) that points from the axis \(z\) to it, by \(s\) times its length. The blue arrow is this displacement \(\mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\), the grey right-angle mark shows that it is perpendicular to the line \(O P\). All four corners move by the same rule, perpendicular to their line from \(O\). The orange square is therefore the plate turned about \(O\). For such a large \(s\) it is also slightly larger than the blackwhite one. The displacement of the point \(P\) is perpendicular to \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(s\,|\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}|\) long, so by the Pythagorean theorem the new distance of \(P\) from \(O\) is \(\sqrt{1 + s^2}\,|\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}|\). The same computation holds for every side of the square. Let the side go from a point \(Q\) to a point \(Q'\) and have the vector \(\vek d = \vek r_{\mathrm{Q}'} - \vek r_{\mathrm{Q}}\) in the plane \(x\)-\(y\), with \(d_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The difference of the displacements of its end points is \(\mat W\) times the vector of the side (lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix), and the sum of the products of its components with the components of \(\vek d\) is zero:

\[\mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{Q}'} - \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{Q}} = \mat W\,\vek d = (-s\,d_{\mathrm{y}},\ s\,d_{\mathrm{x}},\ 0) , \qquad d_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot (-s\,d_{\mathrm{y}}) + d_{\mathrm{y}} \cdot s\,d_{\mathrm{x}} = 0 .\]

The difference of the displacements of the end points is therefore perpendicular to the side and \(s\,|\vek d|\) long, so by the Pythagorean theorem the new length of the side is \(\sqrt{1 + s^2}\,|\vek d|\). The sides lengthen \(\sqrt{1 + s^2}\) times, at \(s = 0{,}3\) by \(4{,}4\) %, and at \(s = 0{,}001\) by only \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\) of their length. The same holds for every antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) and every vector \(\vek d\), \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} d_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\mat W\vek d)_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\), which we proved in corollary 1.104 on the double sum and the antisymmetric part, item 1.

On the right is the same square with the corner \(O\), the point \(P\), the line \(O P\) and the blue arrow, which as on the left shows the displacement of \(P\) in the rotation. The grey dashed square is the square after the rotation, the orange square from the left. To all points we add also the constant shift \(\vek a\), drawn at \(O\) and at the turned point \(P\), at the end of the blue arrow. The term \(\vek a\) is the same vector at all points, so it moves all points equally far in the same direction and changes no distance. The orange square on the right, the plate after the rotation and the shift, is therefore the grey dashed square, only moved by \(\vek a\), equally large.

The field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) is therefore not an exact rigid-body displacement. Let us compare it with the exact rotation of section 1.17.6, with the same \(s\):

exact rotation field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\)
fibre lengths stay exactly the same lengthen \(\sqrt{1 + s^2}\) times
small strain tensor \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = c - 1\) exactly \(\mat 0\)
error at \(s = 0{,}001\) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), the length does not change \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), the length grows by \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\)

The lengthening of the side is a term of second order in \(s\). We multiply and divide the difference \(\sqrt{1 + s^2} - 1\) by \(\sqrt{1 + s^2} + 1\) and get

\[\sqrt{1 + s^2} - 1 = \frac{s^2}{\sqrt{1 + s^2} + 1} , \qquad s = 0{,}001: \quad \frac{10^{-6}}{2{,}0000005} = 5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7} ,\]

so a little less than \(s^2/2\). Both displacements are therefore rigid to first order and differ only by terms with \(s^2\). The theorem of this section is about the field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), about displacements whose small strain tensor is exactly zero, not about the exact rotation. Such a field can be added to every displacement field without the small strain tensor changing anywhere: the partial derivative of a sum is the sum of the partial derivatives (lemma 1.81), so the small strain tensor of the sum of two fields is the sum of their tensors, and the second is \(\mat 0\). By the theorem we will test it on the square plate of figure 1.465.

The goal of this section is to show the converse: a displacement field whose small strain tensor is zero at every point of a body has the form \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\). From this the answer to the question at the start will follow. Two displacement fields that have the same strains at every point differ only by \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), that is, by a shift of all points and a small rotation of the body as a whole. There are three assumptions. The displacement field is continuously differentiable (definition 1.90), as we have assumed all along since section 1.15.6. We look at it at the interior points of the body, which form an open set (lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point). The body is in one piece. We will write the last assumption precisely, because without it the claim fails. Let us write the route as a list, with the purpose of each step:

  1. The lemma on the derivatives of the rotation: what the strains say about the rotation when the field has continuous second partial derivatives. We test it on the hanging bar. The theorem bypasses it, but we need it in the next section, where we will look for the rotation by summing along a path.
  2. Two separate cubes: an example that shows why the body must be in one piece.
  3. The distance to the points of a segment: a segment between two points of a ball stays in the ball. The proof will use the strains along such segments, so they must lie in the body.
  4. The exact statement of the words "in one piece" and the ring as an example of such a body with a hole.
  5. The derivative along a segment: with it we differentiate the displacement along a segment in the first step of the proof.
  6. A function with zero partial derivatives is constant on a set in one piece: with it we carry the result from a small ball to the whole body.
  7. The theorem and its test on the turned plate, then the meaning for the hanging bar and for a body with a hole.

The partial derivatives of the displacement contain the strain and the rotation, \(\mat H = \ten\varepsilon + \ten\omega\) (section 1.17.5). What do the strains say about the rotation? Not its values, since the field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) has zero strains and the rotation \(\mat W\), which can be any antisymmetric matrix. How the rotation changes from point to point, though, is determined by the strains, when the displacement field has continuous second partial derivatives.

Let us show this first on the hanging bar, so we repeat its field. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, the axis \(x\) points vertically down from the centre \(O\) of the top end, so \(x\) is the depth, and the axis \(y\) is perpendicular to the bar and measures the distance from the axis. The number \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) is from section 1.2. By (1.18) the components of the displacement are

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y .\]

The number \(0{,}6\) is \(0{,}3 \cdot 2\): the strain along the axis is \(2a\,(L - x)\), and the transverse one is \(-0{,}3\) times it, where \(0{,}3\) is the Poisson number of steel (section 1.6). The partial derivatives that we need are

\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} = -0{,}6\,a\,y , \qquad \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} = +0{,}6\,a\,y , \qquad \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) .\]

For \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) the sign is positive, because \(-(L - x) = x - L\) has the derivative \(+1\) with respect to \(x\). From them we get

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y + 0{,}6\,a\,y) = 0 , \\ \omega_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y - 0{,}6\,a\,y) = -0{,}6\,a\,y . \end{aligned}\]

Let us draw both functions (figure 1.451) with two graphs. On the left graph the horizontal axis is the depth \(x\) up to the end of the bar at \(L\), and the vertical axis is the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The line is \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\): at \(x = 0\) it has the value \(-0{,}6\,a\,L\), at \(x = L\) zero. On the right graph the horizontal axis is the coordinate \(y\), measured from the axis of the bar, and the vertical one is the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The line \(-0{,}6\,a\,y\) goes through the origin and falls. The blue triangle on the left measures the slope of the strain. Its horizontal leg is \(\Delta x\), the vertical one \(0{,}6\,a\,\Delta x\), so the slope is \(0{,}6\,a\). The blue triangle on the right measures the slope of the rotation. Its horizontal leg is \(\Delta y\), and the vertical one \(-0{,}6\,a\,\Delta y\), negative because the line falls. The slope is therefore \(-0{,}6\,a\). The slopes are equal in size and opposite in sign. For the hanging bar, where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), the lemma below will say this: \(\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} / \partial y = -\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} / \partial x\). The scales of the axes differ on the graphs. On the left graph the length of the bar, 10 m, is drawn horizontally, on the right its diameter, 10 mm. So the lines do not look equally steep.

Lemma 1.128 Derivatives of the rotation from derivatives of the strains (odvodi zasuka iz odvodov deformacij)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, and let the components \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) of a displacement field have at every point of \(D\) partial derivatives of first and second order that are continuous at every point of \(D\). Let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be the components of the small strain tensor (definition 1.115) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\) the components of the small rotation tensor (definition 1.116), where the indices \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k}\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and let \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\) and \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). Then at every point of \(D\), for all \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k}\) we have:

  1. the partial derivatives of the rotation are differences of partial derivatives of the strains,
    \[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} , \tag{1.69}\]
  2. the second partial derivatives of the displacements are sums of partial derivatives of the strains and the rotation,
    \[\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} + \frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} + \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
Proof

We have to show that the two sides of both equalities agree when the components of the strain and the rotation are written with partial derivatives of the displacements. We compute partial derivatives as ordinary derivatives, so the two rules of lemma 1.81 hold for them: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant factor can be taken out.

1. Derivatives of the rotation.

  1. By definition 1.116, \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\). We differentiate with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) and get, by definition 1.124,
    \[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
  2. By definition 1.115, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\). We differentiate the first with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\), the second with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\), and write the difference:
    \[\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} + \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} - \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}} - \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} .\]
  3. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\). Since \(D\) is open, all points at a distance less than some number \(r > 0\) from \(P\) are in \(D\). At them the first and second partial derivatives of the displacements exist, and at \(P\) they are continuous. So by theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives, the order of two differentiations does not matter at \(P\). When the indices of both differentiations are equal, for example \(\ix{j} = \ix{k}\) in the first term, the derivative is the same in both orders and swapping changes nothing. We therefore rearrange the four terms on the right of step 2 as follows, from left to right:
term from step 2 after swapping the order of differentiation what happens to it
\(+\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}\) \(+\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}\) stays, the first term on the right of step 1
\(+\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\) \(+\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}\) the same derivative as in the fourth term, they cancel
\(-\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}\) \(-\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\) stays, the second term on the right of step 1
\(-\tfrac12\,\dfrac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}\) no swap cancels with the second term

The first and the third term remain:

\[\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} - \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{j}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}} .\]
  1. The right side is the right side of step 1, so (1.69) holds.

2. Second derivatives of the displacements.

  1. By section 1.17.5, \(\mat H = \ten\varepsilon + \ten\omega\), entry by entry \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  2. We differentiate both sides with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\). The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, so we get the first equality of item 2. We get the second when we replace \(\partial\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\) by (1.69).

Source: SADD (2.6.6) (PDF p. 52), written with commas for partial derivatives, \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij},\mathrm{k}} = e_{\mathrm{ik},\mathrm{j}} - e_{\mathrm{jk},\mathrm{i}}\), and with the same sign of the rotation as ours (SADD (2.1.7), PDF p. 40). The proof follows the source, and we justify swapping the order of differentiation by the theorem on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives.

The lemma says that the rotation cannot change arbitrarily: how fast it changes in the direction of the axis \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) is determined by derivatives of the strains. Let us test it on the hanging bar, whose derivatives we wrote before the lemma. The rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}6\,a\,y\) has the derivative \(-0{,}6\,a\) with respect to \(y\). Item 1 of the lemma with \(\ix{i} = x\), \(\ix{j} = y\) and \(\ix{k} = y\) gives the same from the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\):

\[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x} = 0 - 0{,}6\,a = -1{,}171 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} .\]

Item 2 of the lemma with the same indices gives the second derivative of the component \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\):

\[\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y^2} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} = 0 - 0{,}6\,a ,\]

and indeed the term \(-0{,}3\,a\,y^2\) in \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) has the second derivative \(-0{,}6\,a\) with respect to \(y\), which is the slope of the line of the rotation, since \(\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}/\partial y = 0\).

Figure 1.100 shows why the rotation changes with \(y\). A point at the distance \(y\) from the axis moves toward the axis by \(0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y\), so more at a smaller depth \(x\). The top end of a vertical fibre therefore moves toward the axis more than the bottom end, and the fibre tilts. In a step downward its point moves away from the axis by \(0{,}6\,a\,y\) times the length of the step, which is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\). The tilt is proportional to \(y\), so the fibres farther from the axis tilt more, and the material turns the more, the farther from the axis it is (the line in figure 1.451). At the point \(P\), 4 mm from the axis, \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}6\,a \cdot 0{,}004\ \text{m} = -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\), as in section 1.17.5.

The lemma also gives a short route to the goal of the section, when the displacement field has continuous second partial derivatives. Let us write it in three steps.

  1. The strains are zero at every point, so their derivatives are zero too. By item 2 of the lemma every second partial derivative of the displacements is therefore zero, \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\).
  2. These are the partial derivatives of the entries of the displacement gradient \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{i}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\). A function with zero partial derivatives is constant on a body in one piece (lemma 1.133 below), so the gradient is the same matrix \(\mat W\) at all points. Its symmetric part is the small strain tensor, which is zero, \(\tfrac12(\mat W + \mat W^\T) = \mat 0\), so \(\mat W\) is antisymmetric.
  3. The function \(u_{\mathrm{i}} - \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}\) therefore has zero partial derivatives and is constant, equal to some number \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\). This is \(\vek u = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), as in steps 16 and 17 of the proof of the theorem below.

This route, however, needs the second partial derivatives of the displacements to exist and be continuous. In chapter 4 we will need the theorem for the difference of two displacement fields, about which we will only know that it is continuously differentiable. So we prove it with first partial derivatives only, and the lemma on the derivatives of the rotation is left for the next section. The idea is geometric and has three steps. Let us draw them (figure 1.452) on the field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) with greatly magnified entries of the matrix \(\mat W\), so that it can be seen. The figure only illustrates what the field looks like for which we will prove that it is the only possibility. It does not replace the argument, the proof uses nothing that it would take from the figure.

The figure has two parts. The left part shows what the proof says about a segment. The grey closed curve is the boundary of the open set \(D\), that is, the body in which the displacement field has no strains. The blackwhite segment from the point \(A\) to the point \(B\) lies in \(D\). On it are five points at equal spacing. The orange segment is the segment after the displacement, shifted and turned. Its length is the same, which holds only to first order, as for the field in figure 1.450. The blue arrows are the displacements of the five points. The grey dashed vertical lines drop the end of each arrow onto the line of the segment, so that it can be seen how far the point moves in the direction of the segment. The grey dimensions below the segment reach from each point to the foot of its vertical line and are all equally long. The right part is drawn on a larger scale around the point \(C\), so that the labels do not overlap the triangle. The grey dashed circle is the ball with centre \(C\) and radius \(\rho\). The ball lies entirely in the body \(D\). The blackwhite triangle has corners \(C\), \(X = C + \vek v\) and \(Y = C + \vek w\). From \(X\) and \(Y\) lead the blue arrows, the differences of displacements \(\vek g(\vek v) = \vek u(X) - \vek u(C)\) and \(\vek g(\vek w) = \vek u(Y) - \vek u(C)\). Both are perpendicular to the side that leads from \(C\) to the same point, as the grey right-angle marks show. On the right we therefore do not draw the displacements but the differences of displacements relative to \(C\): from all points we subtracted the displacement \(\vek u(C)\). So the point \(C\) stays in place. The orange triangle is the triangle after the displacement, turned about \(C\).

  1. The segment. Zero strain means that no short fibre gets longer to first order. We will show that therefore not even a long segment in the body gets longer to first order. Let the segment from \(A\) to \(B\) have the vector \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{AB}\), and let \(\Delta\vek u = \vek u(B) - \vek u(A)\) be the difference of the displacements of its end points. After loading the segment has the vector \(\vek d + \Delta\vek u\), and we expand the square of its length as in section 1.17.5:
    \[|\vek d + \Delta\vek u|^2 = |\vek d|^2 + 2\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \Delta u_{\mathrm{i}}\,d_{\mathrm{i}} + |\Delta\vek u|^2 .\]
    The first term is the square of the length before loading, the last is the square of a small number. The first-order change is the middle term, twice the sum, for which we will show
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(u_{\mathrm{i}}(B) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(A)\big)\,d_{\mathrm{i}} = 0 .\]
    A sum equal to zero says that the segment does not get longer to first order: the difference of the displacements of the end points has no component in the direction of the segment, it is perpendicular to it. The same holds for every part of the segment, for example from \(A\) to a point \(T\) on it, since this is also a segment in the body. Every point \(T\) of the segment therefore moves in the direction of the segment equally far as \(A\), like the points of a rigid rod (grey dimensions, all equally long).
  2. A triangle in a ball. Around the point \(C\) we take a ball of radius \(\rho\) that lies entirely in the body. For every vector \(\vek v\) shorter than \(\rho\) the point \(C + \vek v\) is in the ball, and we denote the difference of the displacements by \(\vek g(\vek v) = \vek u(C + \vek v) - \vek u(C)\) (blue arrows). Step 1 holds for all three sides of every triangle with the corner \(C\) in the ball. No side gets longer to first order, so the triangle only moves and turns. We will derive that \(\vek g(\vek v)\) is the product of an antisymmetric matrix with the vector \(\vek v\). We denote this matrix by \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\), because it depends on the chosen point \(C\). The number \(\lambda\) in the third row is arbitrary, only \(\lambda\,\vek v\) must be shorter than \(\rho\). The way there has five conclusions:
    \[\begin{aligned} & \textstyle\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} && \text{(sides of the triangle, step 8)} \\ \Longrightarrow\ & \vek g(\vek v + \vek w) = \vek g(\vek v) + \vek g(\vek w) && \text{(sum, step 10)} \\ & \vek g(\lambda\,\vek v) = \lambda\,\vek g(\vek v) && \text{(multiple, step 11)} \\ & \vek g(\vek v) = \mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,\vek v && \text{(matrix, step 12)} \\ & \mat W_{\mathrm{C}}^\T = -\mat W_{\mathrm{C}} && \text{(antisymmetry, step 13)} \end{aligned}\]
    The first row follows from step 1 for the three sides of the triangle with end points \(C\), \(C + \vek v\) and \(C + \vek w\), the others from the first. The step numbers are the steps of the proof below.
  3. So the displacement gradient is constant near every point \(C\), equal to \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\). For it to be the same in the whole body we need that from every point of the body we can reach every other one along a path in the body.

What it means for a body to be in one piece, and why it matters, is shown by an example (figure 1.453). Two steel cubes with an edge of 10 mm lie on a table, separated by a gap.

Let us draw this from the front (figure 1.453). The axis \(x\) points from the left cube to the right, with coordinates in millimetres. We leave the left cube, a blackwhite square from \(0\) to \(10\) mm, in place. The right cube before the shift is a blackwhite square from \(20\) to \(30\) mm, and the right one after the shift is an orange square. We shift it as a whole by 1 mm in the direction of the axis \(x\). The blue arrows measure this shift at the left and right edge of the cube, it is the same everywhere. In the figure the shift is four times longer than it would be on the scale of the cubes, so that it can be seen. The grey segment from \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) to \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the empty circle above the label \(15\) belong to a broken line that we will define below, and we explain them there. Let us write the displacement field on the board, in millimetres:

\[\vek u(P) = (0, 0, 0) \ \text{ for } P \text{ in the left cube} , \qquad \vek u(P) = (1, 0, 0) \ \text{ for } P \text{ in the right cube} .\]

Around every point the displacement is constant, so all partial derivatives and all strains are zero. But the field is not of the form \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) with the same \(\vek a\) and \(\mat W\) in both cubes. Suppose that it is, and let us argue in three lines.

  1. In the left cube take the points \(P\) and \(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\). The left side of the equality \(\vek u(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) - \vek u(P) = \mat W\,(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\) is \(\vek 0\), the right side is \(h\) times the column \(\ix{j}\) of the matrix \(\mat W\) (definition 1.96). All columns are zero, \(\mat W = \mat 0\).
  2. In the left cube we therefore have \(\vek 0 = \vek u(P) = \vek a + \mat 0\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = \vek a\), so \(\vek a = \vek 0\).
  3. At a point \(Q\) of the right cube the displacement would then be \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{Q}} = \vek 0\), but it is \((1, 0, 0)\) mm. This is a contradiction.

Each cube moves rigidly, but each in its own way, with a different \(\vek a\). The theorem must therefore require the body to be in one piece, and we will write this with segments.

The segment from a point \(A\) to a point \(B\) is the set of points \(A + t\,\overrightarrow{AB}\) for the numbers \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\). At \(t = 0\) we are at \(A\), at \(t = 1\) at \(B\) ((1.8)). The proof will take two points in a ball around a point \(C\) and use, for the segment between them, that it does not get longer to first order. It may do so only if the whole segment lies in the ball and so in the body, otherwise the strains on it are not zero. So we ask: how far are the points of the segment from a given point \(C\)?

Let us draw this (figure 1.454). The blackwhite segment has the ends \(A\) and \(B\), and its length is \(|AB|\). Outside it is the point \(C\). The point \(T\) on the segment is for \(t = 0{,}6\), as the grey dimensions under the segment show: from \(A\) to \(T\) it is \(t\,|AB|\), and from \(T\) to \(B\) it is \((1 - t)\,|AB|\). We look for the distance \(|CT|\), the blue line, expressed by the distances to the ends, the grey lines \(|CA|\) and \(|CB|\), and by the length of the segment. The grey dashed circle is a ball with centre \(C\) and radius \(\rho\) in which \(A\) and \(B\) lie. Beside each line its length is written. We will need the answer twice. For the ball, item 3 of the lemma below will say that the segment stays in the ball. For the ring, item 2 will say that the segment between two nearby points of the middle circle does not come too close to the inner edge of the ring (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.131).

Lemma 1.129 Distance to the points of a segment (razdalja do točk daljice)

Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be points, \(t\) a number and \(T = A + t\,\overrightarrow{AB}\). Then:

  1. the square of the distance from \(C\) to \(T\) is
    \[|CT|^2 = (1 - t)\,|CA|^2 + t\,|CB|^2 - t\,(1 - t)\,|AB|^2 , \tag{1.70}\]
  2. \(t\,(1 - t) \le \tfrac14\), so \(|CT|^2 \ge (1 - t)\,|CA|^2 + t\,|CB|^2 - \tfrac14\,|AB|^2\),
  3. if \(0 \le t \le 1\) and \(A\) and \(B\) are at a distance less than some number \(\rho > 0\) from \(C\), then \(T\) is also at a distance less than \(\rho\) from \(C\).
Proof

We have to show the equality of item 1 and then get from it the inequalities of items 2 and 3.

1. The equality.

  1. The coordinate \(x\) of the point \(T\) is \(x_{\mathrm{A}} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{B}} - x_{\mathrm{A}})\) (definition 1.14). Let us draw it (figure 1.455, left): on the number line are the coordinates of the points \(C\), \(A\), \(B\) and \(T\). Let \(p = x_{\mathrm{A}} - x_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(q = x_{\mathrm{B}} - x_{\mathrm{C}}\). Then \(x_{\mathrm{B}} - x_{\mathrm{A}} = q - p\) and \(x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{C}} = p + t\,(q - p) = (1 - t)\,p + t\,q\), where \(t\,(q - p)\) is the distance from \(A\) to \(T\).
  2. We square: \((x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{C}})^2 = (1 - t)^2\,p^2 + 2t\,(1 - t)\,p\,q + t^2\,q^2\).
  3. The right side of (1.70) has for the coordinate \(x\) the part
    \[(1 - t)\,p^2 + t\,q^2 - t\,(1 - t)\,(q - p)^2 .\]
    We expand the square of the difference, \((q - p)^2 = q^2 - 2p\,q + p^2\), and collect the terms with the same product:
    \[\begin{aligned} p^2 &: \quad (1 - t) - t\,(1 - t) = (1 - t)^2 , \\ q^2 &: \quad t - t\,(1 - t) = t^2 , \\ p\,q &: \quad -t\,(1 - t) \cdot (-2) = 2t\,(1 - t) . \end{aligned}\]
    This is the expression of step 2.
  4. The same holds for the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The square of the distance is the sum of the squares of the differences of the coordinates ((1.10)), so we add the three equalities and get (1.70).

2. Lower bound.

  1. We expand \(\tfrac14 - t\,(1 - t) = t^2 - t + \tfrac14 = \big(t - \tfrac12\big)^2\). A square is not negative, so \(t\,(1 - t) \le \tfrac14\). On the right of figure 1.455 is the graph of the function \(t\,(1 - t)\) on the axes \(t\) and \(t\,(1 - t)\), its peak at \(t = \tfrac12\) is \(\tfrac14\).
  2. The number \(|AB|^2\) is not negative, so \(t\,(1 - t)\,|AB|^2 \le \tfrac14\,|AB|^2\): the largest value \(\tfrac14\) from the figure, multiplied by \(|AB|^2\). Putting this into (1.70) gives the inequality of item 2.

3. A point in the ball.

  1. For \(0 \le t \le 1\) the point \(T\) lies between \(A\) and \(B\), the numbers \(t\) and \(1 - t\) are not negative, so the last term in (1.70) is not positive, and \(|CT|^2 \le (1 - t)\,|CA|^2 + t\,|CB|^2\).
  2. By the assumption and by lemma 1.28 that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(|CA|^2 < \rho^2\) and \(|CB|^2 < \rho^2\). The numbers \(1 - t\) and \(t\) are not negative and at least one of them is positive, so \((1 - t)\,|CA|^2 + t\,|CB|^2 < (1 - t)\,\rho^2 + t\,\rho^2 = \rho^2\).
  3. By steps 1 and 2, \(|CT|^2 < \rho^2\), and by the same lemma \(|CT| < \rho\).

Source: The lemma is not from a source.

Item 3 says that a ball, that is, the set of all points at a distance less than \(\rho\) from a point \(C\), contains together with every two of its points also the segment between them. Item 1 says something more about a circle. If \(A\) and \(B\) are different points at the distance \(\rho\) from \(C\), then for \(0 < t < 1\) the distance \(|CT|^2 = \rho^2 - t\,(1 - t)\,|AB|^2\) is smaller than \(\rho^2\). All points of the segment between them are therefore closer to \(C\) than \(\rho\), and none except the ends lies on the circle or the sphere of radius \(\rho\).

Now we can state when a set is in one piece. We want to get from point to point along a path of straight pieces that does not leave the set. Let us draw this in the plane (figure 1.456).

The grey closed curve is the boundary of the C-shaped set \(D\). The point \(P\) is in the lower arm, the point \(Q\) in the upper one. The straight segment from \(P\) to \(Q\), grey dashed, goes across the opening of the C, where points are not in \(D\), so we cannot walk along it. The blue line goes from \(P\) to the point \(A_1\) in the left part, then to the point \(A_2\) and from there to \(Q\). All three segments lie in \(D\). We label the points in order \(A_0 = P\), \(A_1\), \(A_2\) and \(A_3 = Q\).

Definition 1.130 Connected open set (povezana odprta množica)

A broken line (lomljena črta) from a point \(P\) to a point \(Q\) is a finite list of points \(P = A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}} = Q\) together with the segments \(A_0 A_1\), \(A_1 A_2\), ..., \(A_{\mathrm{m}-1} A_{\mathrm{m}}\), where the segment \(AB\) is the set of points \(A + t\,\overrightarrow{AB}\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\). An open set of points \(D\) is connected (povezana) if every two of its points \(P\) and \(Q\) can be joined by a broken line that lies entirely in \(D\).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.6 (PDF p. 419), where this explains what a connected open set in space means, and KREYSZIG §13.3 (PDF p. 646) for sets in the plane.

This is one form of the general notion of connectedness (LEBL1 Def. 7.2.13 and Prop. 7.2.14, PDF p. 268), which for open sets in space is equivalent to the general one. We will use only this form. It suits only open sets, though. On a circle, for example, by item 1 of lemma 1.129 no segment with two different ends lies, so two of its points cannot be joined by a broken line in the circle, although the circle is in one piece.

Which bodies are connected? If a set contains together with every two points also the segment between them, a broken line of a single segment is enough. This is so for a ball by item 3 of lemma 1.129. It is so for a box with edges along the axes, because the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{A}} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{B}} - x_{\mathrm{A}})\) of a point of the segment lies between \(x_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{B}}\) for \(0 \le t \le 1\), and likewise for \(y\) and \(z\). It is also so for a cylinder with axis \(x\) and radius \(R\), for example the round hanging bar. Let \(A\) and \(B\) be in the cylinder and \(T = A + t\,\overrightarrow{AB}\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\). The coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{T}}\) lies between \(x_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{B}}\). The distance of a point from the axis \(x\) depends only on its coordinates \(y\) and \(z\), so we look at the points along the axis \(x\) (figure 1.457).

The blackwhite circle is the cross-section of the cylinder with radius \(R\) around the axis \(O\), and the axes \(y\) and \(z\) lie in the plane of the cross-section. The points \(A' = (0, y_{\mathrm{A}}, z_{\mathrm{A}})\) and \(B' = (0, y_{\mathrm{B}}, z_{\mathrm{B}})\) are \(A\) and \(B\) seen along the axis, and they lie in the circle because \(A\) and \(B\) are in the cylinder. The point \(T' = (0, y_{\mathrm{T}}, z_{\mathrm{T}})\) has the coordinates \(y_{\mathrm{T}} = y_{\mathrm{A}} + t\,(y_{\mathrm{B}} - y_{\mathrm{A}})\) and \(z_{\mathrm{T}} = z_{\mathrm{A}} + t\,(z_{\mathrm{B}} - z_{\mathrm{A}})\), so it is the point of the segment \(A'B'\) at the same \(t\). By item 3 of lemma 1.129 with \(C = O\) and \(\rho = R\), the distance \(|OT'|\), which is the distance of \(T\) from the axis, is less than \(R\). The point \(T\) is therefore in the cylinder.

The two separate cubes of figure 1.453 are not connected. The left cube reaches from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 10\) mm, the right one from \(x = 20\) mm to \(x = 30\) mm (coordinates on the axis \(x\)). Suppose that a broken line in the set joins a point of the left cube to a point of the right one. The points \(A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}}\) of the list that determines it lie in the set, so each in one of the cubes. Let \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the first of them that lies in the right cube. The point \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) before it lies in the left one (the grey segment between them). On this segment, with \(A = A_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) and \(B = A_{\mathrm{k}}\), the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{A}} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{B}} - x_{\mathrm{A}})\) goes from less than \(10\) mm to more than \(20\) mm and equals \(15\) mm at some \(t\). The point with this coordinate is the empty circle, which the grey dashed line drops to the axis at \(15\) mm. It is empty because the point is in neither cube. The segment \(A_{\mathrm{k}-1} A_{\mathrm{k}}\) therefore does not lie in the set, but the broken line would have to lie in it entirely. This is a contradiction, so there is no such broken line, and the set of two cubes is not connected.

A body with a hole, though, can be connected too. Such is the ring, the simplest body with a hole (figure 1.459). Why we care about its connectedness is shown by an example from the next section, which we only hint at here with figure 1.458. We cut the ring from the inner to the outer edge, along the line of the cut. To the cut ring we prescribe strains that it accepts by the cut opening into a wedge-shaped gap. We will ask whether the same strains can be accepted by the whole ring too, where the gap would have to close. The answer will be no, although the strains will satisfy the compatibility equations at every point of the ring. The reason is that the displacements of the cut ring are determined by the strains up to a rigid motion \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), which is continuous across the cut too and does not change the difference between the two sides of the cut. This will follow from a corollary of this section that holds only for connected bodies. If the cut ring were not connected, its parts could move each with its own \(\vek a\) and \(\mat W\), like the two cubes above, and the gap could close. So we prove the connectedness of the cut ring now, together with the connectedness of the whole ring, which we need in chapter 4.

Let us draw the ring. Both parts of the figure show the ring from above. The two blackwhite circles are its inner edge with radius 40 mm and its outer edge with radius 60 mm, the point \(O\) is the common centre. The thick grey line is the cut, which goes along the positive axis \(x\) from the inner to the outer edge. On the right the ring is cut. On the left the ring is whole, and the thick line there only marks the points that the cut ring does not have. A broken line is made of straight segments, so we cannot walk along a circular arc around the hole. We walk along chords. The grey dashed circle with radius 50 mm lies in the middle of the ring. On it are eight grey dots \(K_1\) to \(K_8\), one on each half-axis and one between every two neighbouring ones, for example \(K_2 = (30, 40)\) mm, which is \(50\) mm from \(O\), since \(30^2 + 40^2 = 50^2\). We write all eight in the proof. The point \(K_1\) lies on the cut: on the left it is a grey dot because it is in the whole ring, on the right an empty circle because the cut ring does not have it. The six grey segments are six of the eight sides of the octagon \(K_1 K_2 \dots K_8\). The sides \(K_8 K_1\) and \(K_1 K_2\) are not drawn, because they touch the cut. Each chord moves away from the circle toward the centre, but because the sides are short, it does not come closer to the centre than 40 mm, which we show with item 2 of the lemma on the distance to the points of a segment (step 2 of the proof). The line in the figure does not need the point \(K_8\). We need it for the points just below the cut (step 4).

On the right we draw how we join the points \(P\) and \(Q\) of the cut ring. The blue broken line goes from \(P\) along a ray from \(O\) to the point \(M\) on the middle circle and then straight to \(K_2\). From there it goes along the sides of the octagon to \(K_7\), straight to the middle circle on the ray from \(O\) through \(Q\), and along this ray to \(Q\). It touches the cut nowhere. In the left figure \(P\) and \(M\) are other points than on the right, but \(Q\) is the same. The neighbourhood of the left \(P\) is too small to be seen. A grey circle encloses it on the left, and the circle between the two parts shows it magnified \(4{,}8\) times. The left \(P\) is on the cut, so not in the cut ring. The grey dashed circle around it is a ball with radius \(4{,}8\) mm that lies entirely in the ring. The point \(P'\) in it is above \(P\) by half of the radius of the ball, so it is in the cut ring. From there the blue line goes along a ray to \(M\) on the middle circle, straight to \(K_2\) and from there along the same route as on the right to \(Q\).

Lemma 1.131 The ring is connected (obroč je povezan)

Lengths are measured in millimetres, \(c > 0\) is a number, and \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{P}}^2}\) is the distance of a point \(P\) from the axis \(z\). Let the ring be the set of points \(P\) with \(40 < \rho_{\mathrm{P}} < 60\) and \(|z_{\mathrm{P}}| < c\), and the cut ring the ring without the points with \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) and \(x_{\mathrm{P}} > 0\). Then both sets are open and connected (definition 1.130).

Proof

We have to show that every point of both sets is an interior point and that every two points can be joined by a broken line in the set. First we join the points of the cut ring, where we avoid the cut, and then the points on the cut. We will use eight points on the circle of radius \(50\) in the plane \(z = 0\),

\[\begin{aligned} K_1 &= (50, 0, 0) , & K_2 &= (30, 40, 0) , & K_3 &= (0, 50, 0) , \\ K_4 &= (-30, 40, 0) , & K_5 &= (-50, 0, 0) , & K_6 &= (-30, -40, 0) , \\ K_7 &= (0, -50, 0) , & K_8 &= (30, -40, 0) , \end{aligned}\]

for which \(30^2 + 40^2 = 50^2\) (figure 1.459).

1. Both sets are open.

  1. The functions \(f(Q) = x_{\mathrm{Q}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{Q}}^2\) and \(z_{\mathrm{Q}}\) are polynomials in the coordinates, so they are continuous at every point (corollary 1.69 on the continuity of sums, products and polynomials in space, item 2). So are the coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{Q}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{Q}}\).
  2. Let \(P\) be a point of the ring. By lemma 1.28, \(1600 < f(P) < 3600\). Let \(\eta\) be the smallest of the positive numbers \(f(P) - 1600\), \(3600 - f(P)\) and \(c - |z_{\mathrm{P}}|\). By the definition of continuity 1.67 there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for every point \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\) the values \(f(Q)\) and \(z_{\mathrm{Q}}\) differ from \(f(P)\) and \(z_{\mathrm{P}}\) by less than \(\eta\).
  3. For such a point, \(1600 < f(Q) < 3600\), so \(40 < \rho_{\mathrm{Q}} < 60\), and by the triangle inequality for numbers \(|z_{\mathrm{Q}}| \le |z_{\mathrm{P}}| + |z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}}| < c\). The point \(Q\) is in the ring, so \(P\) is an interior point of the ring.
  4. For a point \(P\) of the cut ring we also reduce \(\eta\) to \(|y_{\mathrm{P}}|\) if \(y_{\mathrm{P}} \neq 0\), and otherwise to \(|x_{\mathrm{P}}|\), since then \(x_{\mathrm{P}} < 0\). We choose the number \(\delta\) for this \(\eta\) so that at the points \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\) also the coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{Q}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{Q}}\) differ from \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\) by less than \(\eta\) (step 1). The points \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\) then have \(y_{\mathrm{Q}}\) of the same sign as \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\), or else \(x_{\mathrm{Q}} < 0\), so they are not on the cut.

2. The cut ring and the ring are connected.

  1. From a point \(P\) of the cut ring we go straight to the point \(M\) \(= \lambda_1\,(x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, 0)\) with \(\lambda_1 = 50/\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\), which lies on the circle of radius \(50\) in the plane \(z = 0\). The points of this segment are \(\big(\lambda\,x_{\mathrm{P}},\ \lambda\,y_{\mathrm{P}},\ (1 - t)\,z_{\mathrm{P}}\big)\) with \(\lambda = (1 - t) + t\,\lambda_1 > 0\). Their distance from the axis \(z\) is \(\lambda\,\rho_{\mathrm{P}} = (1 - t)\,\rho_{\mathrm{P}} + 50\,t\) and lies between \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(50\), and \(|(1 - t)\,z_{\mathrm{P}}| \le |z_{\mathrm{P}}| < c\), so they are in the ring. The coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) are multiplied by the positive number \(\lambda\) and keep their signs, so the segment does not meet the cut.
  2. Let \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) be points in the plane \(z = 0\) at the distance \(50\) from \(O\), with \(|M_1 M_2|^2 < 3600\). For a point \(T\) of the segment between them, by items 1 and 2 of lemma 1.129 with \(C = O\),
    \[2500 - \tfrac14\,|M_1 M_2|^2 \le |OT|^2 \le 2500 ,\]
    so \(1600 < |OT|^2 \le 2500\). The point \(T\) lies in the plane \(z = 0\), so \(|OT| = \rho_{\mathrm{T}}\), and \(40 < \rho_{\mathrm{T}} \le 50\). The segment lies in the ring. The number \(3600\) is chosen because \(2500 - \tfrac14 \cdot 3600 = 1600 = 40^2\): a chord of the middle circle shorter than \(60\) does not come closer to \(O\) than the inner edge.
  3. The squares of the distances between consecutive points \(K_1, K_2, \dots, K_8, K_1\) are \(2000\) or \(1000\), for example \(|K_1 K_2|^2 = 20^2 + 40^2 = 2000\) and \(|K_2 K_3|^2 = 30^2 + 10^2 = 1000\). By step 2 all these segments are in the ring. A coordinate of a point of a segment lies between the coordinates of the ends. The segments \(K_2 K_3\) and \(K_3 K_4\) therefore have \(y > 0\) everywhere, the segments \(K_4 K_5\) and \(K_5 K_6\) have \(x < 0\) everywhere, and the segments \(K_6 K_7\) and \(K_7 K_8\) have \(y < 0\) everywhere. The broken line \(K_2, K_3, \dots, K_8\) is therefore in the cut ring, since it does not touch the cut.

Step 4 joins every point \(M\) of the middle circle to one of the points \(K_2, \dots, K_8\). The chord must have its squared length below \(3600\) for step 2 to hold, and it must not hit the cut. Let us draw the choice (figure 1.460). The ring with the cut, the middle circle and the centre \(O\) is as before. The grey dashed lines \(y = x\) and \(y = -x\) divide the plane into four sectors: the right one with \(x \ge |y|\), the upper one with \(y \ge |x|\), the left one with \(-x \ge |y|\) and the lower one with \(-y \ge |x|\). Every point lies in at least one of them. In each sector we choose a point of the middle circle: \(K_3\) above, \(K_5\) on the left, \(K_7\) below, and in the right one \(K_2\) above the cut and \(K_8\) below it, because a chord must not cross the cut. The blue segments are chords from a few points of the middle circle to the chosen point: from the point \(M\) to \(K_2\), from a point below the cut to \(K_8\), from a point above to \(K_3\), on the left to \(K_5\) and below to \(K_7\). The grey vertical line is the line \(x = 35\). The lines \(y = \pm x\) cut the middle circle at \(x = 50/\sqrt2 = 35{,}4\), so the whole right quarter of the middle circle lies to the right of the vertical line. Instead of \(35\), every number \(x_0\) with \(x_0^2 \le 1250\) for which \(5000 - 60\,x_0 < 3600\) would do, that is \(x_0 > 1400/60\), which is a little more than \(23{,}3\). We choose the round number \(35\).

  1. Let \(M\) be a point of the cut ring on the circle of radius \(50\) in the plane \(z = 0\), as in step 1. Since it lies on this circle, \(x_{\mathrm{M}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{M}}^2 = 2500\), and we use this when we expand the squares. Let first \(M\) be in the right sector, \(x_{\mathrm{M}} \ge |y_{\mathrm{M}}|\). Then \(2x_{\mathrm{M}}^2 \ge x_{\mathrm{M}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{M}}^2 = 2500\), so \(x_{\mathrm{M}}^2 \ge 1250 > 35^2\) and \(x_{\mathrm{M}} > 35\), to the right of the grey vertical line. The point \(M\) is not on the cut, so \(y_{\mathrm{M}} \neq 0\). For \(y_{\mathrm{M}} > 0\) we join it to \(K_2\):
    \[\begin{aligned} |M K_2|^2 &= (x_{\mathrm{M}} - 30)^2 + (y_{\mathrm{M}} - 40)^2 = 5000 - 60\,x_{\mathrm{M}} - 80\,y_{\mathrm{M}} \\ &< 5000 - 60 \cdot 35 = 2900 < 3600 , \end{aligned}\]
    and for \(y_{\mathrm{M}} < 0\) to \(K_8\), where \(|M K_8|^2 = 5000 - 60\,x_{\mathrm{M}} + 80\,y_{\mathrm{M}} < 2900\). By step 2 the segment lies in the ring, and since both ends have \(y > 0\) or both have \(y < 0\), the whole segment has that sign, so it does not hit the cut. In the upper sector, \(y_{\mathrm{M}} \ge |x_{\mathrm{M}}|\), we likewise have \(y_{\mathrm{M}} > 35\) and \(|M K_3|^2 = x_{\mathrm{M}}^2 + (y_{\mathrm{M}} - 50)^2 = 5000 - 100\,y_{\mathrm{M}} < 1500\), and the segment has \(y > 0\) everywhere. In the left and lower sector we likewise have \(|M K_5|^2 = 5000 + 100\,x_{\mathrm{M}} < 1500\) and \(|M K_7|^2 = 5000 + 100\,y_{\mathrm{M}} < 1500\), the segments are in the ring and have \(x < 0\) and \(y < 0\) everywhere, respectively.
  2. For points \(P\) and \(Q\) of the cut ring we put together a broken line from step 1 from \(P\) to \(M_{\mathrm{P}}\), from step 4 from \(M_{\mathrm{P}}\) to one of the points \(K_2, \dots, K_8\), by step 3 to the point \(K_{\mathrm{j}}\) that belongs to the point \(Q\), and from steps 4 and 1 in reverse order to \(Q\) (the blue broken line in figure 1.459, right). The cut ring is connected.
  3. Let \(P\) be a point of the ring. If \(P\) is not on the cut, it is in the cut ring. If it is on the cut, by part 1 there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that all points with \(|PQ| < \delta\) are in the ring (the small ball in the figure on the left), among them \(P' = P + (0, \delta/2, 0)\) with \(y_{\mathrm{P}'} > 0\). The segment \(PP'\) is in the ring, because its points are at most \(\delta/2\) from \(P\), and \(P'\) is in the cut ring. So every point of the ring is joined to the cut ring by a short segment or by none, and in the cut ring step 5 applies. The ring is connected.

Source: The lemma is not from a source.

Now we need one more tool, for the first step of the proof. There we will differentiate the sum \(\varphi(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} u_{\mathrm{i}}(A + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\) with respect to \(t\). The difference \(\varphi(1) - \varphi(0)\) is exactly the sum from step 1 of the idea, which we want to show equal to zero. Along the segment from \(P\) in the direction of the vector \(\vek d\), like the segment from \(A\) to \(B\) in figure 1.452, the function \(f\) of three variables is a function of one variable, \(g(t) = f(P + t\,\vek d)\), where \(t\) tells where on the segment we are (figure 1.461). For a step along an axis its derivative was a partial derivative (lemma 1.87 on the change over a step along an axis). In an arbitrary direction \(\vek d\) we expect, as in corollary 1.92 on the difference of displacements along a fibre, the sum of products of the partial derivatives with the components of the direction:

\[g'(t) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,d_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,d_{\mathrm{y}} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\,d_{\mathrm{z}} ,\]

where the partial derivatives are taken at the point \(P + t\,\vek d\). The lemma below says this.

Let us draw this (figure 1.461). The figure has two parts. On the left is the plane, seen from above. The grey region is the open set \(D\). The segment goes from the point \(P\) to the point \(P + \vek d\), the vector \(\vek d\) above it is its direction and length. The point \(S = P + t\,\vek d\) is on the segment, the ball around it is the grey dashed circle, which stays in \(D\) because \(D\) is open. The point \(Q\) is a step \(s\,\vek d\) ahead of \(S\), so \(Q = P + (t + s)\,\vek d\). Drawn are \(t = 0{,}4\) and \(s = 0{,}3\). The step is shorter than the radius of the ball, so \(Q\) lies in it. On the right is the function of one variable \(g(t)\) along the segment. The horizontal axis is \(t\), which shows where on the segment we are, and the vertical axis is the value of the function. The blackwhite curve is \(g\). The grey dashed vertical lines and labels show the values \(t\) and \(t + s\), the same as on the left, and the dots the corresponding points on the curve, \(g(t) = f(S)\) and \(g(t + s) = f(Q)\). The blue line is the tangent at the point at \(t\). We denote its slope by \(m\). The proof below will write \(m\) with the partial derivatives of \(f\) at \(S\) and show that this really is the slope of the tangent, \(g'(t)\). The blue dimension \(m\,s\) is by how much the tangent rises over the step \(s\), and the orange dimension \(R\) is the remainder: by that much the curve at \(t + s\) exceeds the tangent.

Lemma 1.132 Derivative along a segment (odvod vzdolž daljice)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(f\) a function of three variables that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90). Let \(P\) be a point and \(\vek d = (d_{\mathrm{x}}, d_{\mathrm{y}}, d_{\mathrm{z}})\) a vector. For every number \(t\) for which the point \(P + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), let \(g(t) = f(P + t\,\vek d)\). Then for every such number \(t\):

  1. the function \(g\) is defined at all numbers at a distance less than some positive number from \(t\), and it is differentiable at \(t\) with the derivative
    \[\begin{aligned} g'(t) &= \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} \\ &= \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{y}} \\ &\quad + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{z}} , \end{aligned} \tag{1.71}\]
  2. the derivative \(g'\) is continuous at \(t\).
Proof

We have to show that the derivative exists, its value, and its continuity. Let \(t\) be a number for which \(S = P + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\).

1. The derivative.

  1. If \(\vek d = \vek 0\), then \(g\) is the constant function with the value \(f(P)\), defined for all numbers. By lemma 1.81 on the rules of differentiation, item 4, its derivative is \(0\), which is also the right side of (1.71). From now on let \(\vek d \neq \vek 0\).
  2. Since \(D\) is open, there is an \(r > 0\) such that all points at a distance less than \(r\) from \(S\) are in \(D\). The point \(P + (t + s)\,\vek d = S + s\,\vek d\) is at the distance \(\sqrt{s^2 d_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + s^2 d_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + s^2 d_{\mathrm{z}}^2} = |s|\,|\vek d|\) from \(S\) ((1.10)). For \(|s| < r/|\vek d|\) it is therefore in \(D\), and \(g\) is defined at all numbers \(t + s\) with \(|s| < r/|\vek d|\).
  3. Let \(0 < |s| < r/|\vek d|\) and \(Q = S + s\,\vek d\). The components of the step from \(S\) to \(Q\) are \(s\,d_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(s\,d_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(s\,d_{\mathrm{z}}\). The function \(f\) is defined at all points at a distance less than \(r\) from \(S\), its partial derivatives exist there and are continuous at \(S\), so theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step holds. The theorem says two things. The change \(f(Q) - f(S)\) is the sum of the products of the partial derivatives at \(S\) with the components of the step and the remainder \(R(Q)\). And for every error \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|R(Q)| \le \eta\,|SQ|\) for every point \(Q\) with \(0 < |SQ| < \delta\). By (1.34),
    \[g(t + s) - g(t) = f(Q) - f(S) = m\,s + R(Q) , \qquad m = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(S)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} .\]
  4. We divide by \(s\). The difference quotient of the function \(g\) at \(t\) is \(m + R(Q)/s\).
  5. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\).
