By the theorem on the change of a field with the error \(\eta/(2|\vek d|)\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|R(Q)| \le \tfrac{\eta}{2|\vek d|}\,|SQ|\) for every point \(Q\) with \(0 < |SQ| < \delta\). Let \(\delta'\) be smaller than the numbers \(\delta/|\vek d|\) and \(r/|\vek d|\). For \(0 < |s| < \delta'\) we have \(0 < |SQ| = |s|\,|\vek d| < \delta\), so
    \[\Big|\frac{g(t + s) - g(t)}{s} - m\Big| = \frac{|R(Q)|}{|s|} \le \frac{\eta}{2|\vek d|} \cdot \frac{|s|\,|\vek d|}{|s|} = \frac{\eta}{2} < \eta .\]
  6. By the definition of the limit 1.5 the limit of the difference quotient is equal to \(m\). By the definition of the derivative 1.9, \(g\) is differentiable at \(t\) and \(g'(t) = m\), which is (1.71).

2. Continuity of the derivative.

  1. For \(\vek d = \vek 0\) the derivative \(g'\) is zero everywhere and therefore continuous. Let \(\vek d \neq \vek 0\). By step 2 of the first part all numbers \(t + s\) with \(|s| < r/|\vek d|\) are such that \(P + (t + s)\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), so by the first part \(g'\) is defined at all of them.
  2. We pick any error \(\eta > 0\). The partial derivatives of \(f\) are continuous at \(S\), so by definition 1.67 there are bands \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{z}}\) for the error \(\eta/(3|\vek d|)\). Let \(\delta'\) be the smallest of the numbers \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}}/|\vek d|\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{y}}/|\vek d|\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{z}}/|\vek d|\) and \(r/|\vek d|\).
  3. For \(|s| < \delta'\) the point \(S + s\,\vek d\) is at the distance \(|s|\,|\vek d|\) from \(S\), which is less than all three bands. Each partial derivative at it differs from its value at \(S\) by less than \(\eta/(3|\vek d|)\).
  4. No component of a vector is longer than the vector, \(|d_{\mathrm{j}}| \le |\vek d|\) (as in step 4 of the proof of theorem 1.88). By the triangle inequality for numbers and by step 3,
    \[\begin{aligned} |g'(t + s) - g'(t)| &\le \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Big|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(S + s\,\vek d) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(S)\Big|\,|d_{\mathrm{j}}| \\ &< 3 \cdot \frac{\eta}{3|\vek d|} \cdot |\vek d| = \eta . \end{aligned}\]
    The difference of the values of \(g'\) is therefore less than \(\eta\).
  5. We picked the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily and found a band \(\delta'\) for it, so by definition 1.58 the derivative \(g'\) is continuous at \(t\).

Source: LEBL2 §8.3 (PDF pp. 41-42) for the directional derivative of a differentiable function, and Prop. 8.4.6 (PDF pp. 48-49), which shows that a function with continuous partial derivatives is differentiable. The proof from the theorem on the change of a field over a short step is not from the source.

For \(\vek d = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) the sum in (1.71) is the partial derivative with respect to \(y\), as in the lemma on the change over a step along an axis. In this chapter we need only item 1 of the lemma. Item 2, the continuity of the derivative, we will need in chapter 4, where we will write the change of a function along a segment as a sum of very small increments, that is, as the integral of its derivative (definition 3.34), for which the derivative must be continuous. Now let us show that a function without change in any direction is constant on a connected set, just as for the bar a function with zero derivative is constant on an interval.

Figure 1.462 has three parts. On the left is the plane, seen from above. The grey closed curve is the boundary of the connected open set \(D\), and the blackwhite segment from \(A\) to \(B\) lies in it. In the middle is the function \(g(t) = f(A + t\,\vek d)\) along this segment, for \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\). The axes are \(t\) and \(g\), the horizontal blackwhite line is the graph of \(g\), horizontal because the derivative is zero. The dots are the values at \(t = 0\) and \(t = 1\), and the grey dashed line shows that they are equal, \(f(A) = f(B)\). On the right is the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) with a vertical axis and the axis of the variable. This part is needed by step 1 of the proof: the lemma on the derivative along a segment requires continuous partial derivatives, and about \(f\) we know only that they are zero. The blackwhite line is its graph, everywhere at zero. The grey dashed lines bound a band of width \(2\eta\) around zero, and the line lies in the band, however narrow it is.

Lemma 1.133 Zero partial derivatives on a connected set (ničelni parcialni odvodi na povezani množici)

Let \(D\) be a connected open set (definition 1.130) and \(f\) a function of three variables defined on \(D\) whose partial derivatives \(\partial f/\partial x\), \(\partial f/\partial y\) and \(\partial f/\partial z\) exist and are equal to zero at every point of \(D\). Then \(f\) is constant on \(D\): \(f(Q) = f(P)\) for every two points \(P\) and \(Q\) of \(D\).

Proof

We have to show that \(f\) does not change along any segment in \(D\), and carry this over to broken lines.

  1. The function \(f\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\). Its partial derivatives exist at every point of \(D\) and are zero, and the function that is zero everywhere is continuous, since the difference of its values is always \(0\), less than any error \(\eta\).
  2. Let \(A\) and \(B\) be points for which the segment \(AB\) lies in \(D\), and \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{AB}\). Let \(g(t) = f(A + t\,\vek d)\) for every \(t\) for which \(A + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), among them all \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\). By lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment, item 1, for every such \(t\) the function \(g\) is defined at all numbers near \(t\), differentiable at \(t\), and \(g'(t) = 0 \cdot d_{\mathrm{x}} + 0 \cdot d_{\mathrm{y}} + 0 \cdot d_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\).
  3. By lemma 1.79 that a differentiable function is continuous, \(g\) is continuous at every \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\). The condition of continuity on the interval \([0, 1]\) checks only numbers of this interval, so \(g\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\) (as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 1.87).
  4. By corollary 1.85 on a function with zero derivative, \(g(1) = g(0)\), that is, \(f(B) = f(A)\).
  5. Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be points of \(D\). By definition 1.130 there is a broken line, like the blue line in figure 1.456, \(P = A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}} = Q\) whose segments lie in \(D\). By step 4, \(f(A_{\mathrm{k}}) = f(A_{\mathrm{k}-1})\) for every \(k\) from \(1\) to \(m\), so \(f(Q) = f(A_{\mathrm{m}}) = f(A_{\mathrm{m}-1}) = \dots = f(A_0) = f(P)\).

Source: LEBL2 Cor. 8.4.4 (PDF p. 47), for connected open sets in the general sense, with a different proof. The proof with a broken line is not from the source.

Now we have everything for the theorem. Its proof follows the idea of figure 1.452: first a segment, then a triangle in a ball, and finally broken lines across the whole body. We draw steps 9 to 13, in which we get the matrix from perpendicularity along segments, just before them (figure 1.463), and steps 14 and 15 in figure 1.464.

Theorem 1.134 A displacement field without strain (polje brez deformacij)

Let \(D\) be a connected open set of points (definition 1.130) and \(\vek u\) a displacement field that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90). For a point \(P\) let \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = \overrightarrow{OP} = (x_{\mathrm{P}}, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) be the vector from the origin \(O\) to \(P\). Then:

  1. if the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek u\) (definition 1.115) is the zero matrix at every point of \(D\), there are a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) such that
    \[\vek u(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} \qquad \text{for every point } P \text{ iz } D , \tag{1.72}\]
  2. conversely, every field of the form (1.72) with a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) has at every point the displacement gradient \(\mat W\) and a zero small strain tensor.
Proof

We have to show that zero strains give the form (1.72), and conversely. The indices \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k}\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\), and \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}(P) = \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,(P)\) are the entries of the displacement gradient \(\mat H(P)\) at the point \(P\) (definition 1.109).

1. Zero strains give the form (1.72).

  1. A segment in \(D\). Let \(A\) and \(B\) be points for which the segment \(AB\) lies in \(D\), and \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{AB}\). For every \(t\) for which \(A + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), let \(\varphi(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} u_{\mathrm{i}}(A + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\). The difference \(\varphi(1) - \varphi(0) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(u_{\mathrm{i}}(B) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(A)\big)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the sum from step 1 of the idea, which we want to show equal to zero.
  2. By lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment, item 1, used for each component \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\), and by the rules for the derivative of a sum and of a multiple (lemma 1.81), for every \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\) the function \(\varphi\) is defined at all numbers near \(t\), differentiable at \(t\), and
    \[\varphi'(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} d_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}(A + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek d^\T\,\mat H(A + t\,\vek d)\,\vek d ,\]
    where we wrote the double sum by (1.41).
  3. By corollary 1.104 on the double sum and the antisymmetric part, item 2, \(\vek d^\T\mat H\,\vek d = \vek d^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek d\), where \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\) is the small strain tensor. It is zero at the point \(A + t\,\vek d\), which lies in \(D\). So \(\varphi'(t) = 0\) for every \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\).
  4. As in steps 3 and 4 of the proof of lemma 1.133, \(\varphi\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\) and \(\varphi(1) = \varphi(0)\) (corollary 1.85). Putting in \(\varphi(1) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} u_{\mathrm{i}}(B)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\varphi(0) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} u_{\mathrm{i}}(A)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}\) we get
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(u_{\mathrm{i}}(B) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(A)\big)\,d_{\mathrm{i}} = 0 . \tag{1.73}\]
  5. A ball. Let \(C\) be a point of \(D\). Since \(D\) is open, there is a number \(\rho > 0\) such that all points at a distance less than \(\rho\) from \(C\) are in \(D\). For a vector \(\vek v\) with \(|\vek v| < \rho\) the point \(C + \vek v\) is at the distance \(|\vek v|\) from \(C\), so it is in \(D\). Let \(\vek g(\vek v) = \vek u(C + \vek v) - \vek u(C)\), with the components \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\).
  6. Let \(\vek v\) and \(\vek w\) be vectors with \(|\vek v| < \rho\) and \(|\vek w| < \rho\), \(X = C + \vek v\) and \(Y = C + \vek w\). The points \(C\), \(X\) and \(Y\) are at a distance less than \(\rho\) from \(C\), so by lemma 1.129 on the distance to the points of a segment, item 3, the segments \(CX\), \(CY\) and \(XY\) lie in the ball and hence in \(D\).
  7. For the segment from \(C\) to \(X\), \(\vek d = \vek v\) and \(\vek u(X) - \vek u(C) = \vek g(\vek v)\). By (1.73), \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\): \(\vek g(\vek v)\) has no part in the direction of \(\vek v\), it is perpendicular to it. Likewise \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) (\(\vek g(\vek w)\)).
  8. For the segment from \(X\) to \(Y\), \(\vek d = \vek w - \vek v\) and \(\vek u(Y) - \vek u(X) = [\vek g(\vek w) - \vek g(\vek v)](@fig-pbd-daljica:gv,gw)\). By (1.73), \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w) - g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\big)(w_{\mathrm{i}} - v_{\mathrm{i}}) = 0\). We expand into four sums, \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} - \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} - \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). The first and the last are zero by step 7, so
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} . \tag{1.74}\]

Let us draw steps 9 to 13 (figure 1.463) on the field \(\vek g(\vek v) = \mat W\vek v\) with an antisymmetric matrix with the entries \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -s\) and \(W_{\mathrm{yx}} = s\), in the plane and with a greatly magnified \(s = 0{,}4\) so that it can be seen. On the left is the sum. The blackwhite vectors \(\vek v\), \(\vek w\) and \(\vek v + \vek w\) lead from the point \(C\). The blue arrows at the ends of the vectors \(\vek v\) and \(\vek w\) are \(\vek g(\vek v)\) and \(\vek g(\vek w)\), and the blue arrow at the end of the sum is \(\vek g(\vek v + \vek w)\). The orange arrows are \(\vek g(\vek v)\) and \(\vek g(\vek w)\), laid one after the other from the end of the sum. They end where \(\vek g(\vek v + \vek w)\) ends, which step 10 claims. In the middle is the multiple. The points \(\vek v\) and \(\lambda\,\vek v\) lie on the same ray from \(C\), and \(\lambda = 2\) is drawn. Their displacements point in the same direction, and the second is \(\lambda\) times longer, which step 11 claims. On the right is the matrix. The blackwhite segments \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) lie along the axes. The blue arrows at their ends are \(\vek g(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\) and \(\vek g(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\). Divided by \(h\), they are the columns of the matrix \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\) (step 12). They are equally long, one pointing up and the other to the left, which is the antisymmetry (step 13). The vector \(\vek v\) is the sum of the parts along the axes, grey dashed, and its displacement is the sum of the corresponding multiples of the two blue arrows.

  1. A sum. Let \(\vek v\), \(\vek w\) and \(\vek v + \vek w\) be shorter than \(\rho\), and let \(\vek m\) be any vector with \(|\vek m| < \rho\). By (1.74), used three times,
    \[\begin{aligned} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v + \vek w)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} &= -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek m)\,(v_{\mathrm{i}} + w_{\mathrm{i}}) \\ &= -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek m)\,v_{\mathrm{i}} - \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek m)\,w_{\mathrm{i}} \\ &= \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} , \end{aligned}\]
    so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v + \vek w) - g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v) - g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek w)\big)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\).
  2. Let \(h = \rho/2\). Any \(h\) with \(0 < h < \rho\) would do, since only the vector \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) must be shorter than \(\rho\). For \(\vek m = h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) only the term with \(\ix{i} = x\) in the sum of step 9 is nonzero, so \(h\,\big(g_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek v + \vek w) - g_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek v) - g_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek w)\big) = 0\), and the bracket is zero. Likewise with \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). So \(\vek g(\vek v + \vek w) = \vek g(\vek v) + \vek g(\vek w)\).
  3. A multiple. Let \(\vek v\) be shorter than \(\rho\) and \(\lambda\) a number for which \(\lambda\,\vek v\) is also shorter than \(\rho\). By (1.74), used twice, for every \(\vek m\) with \(|\vek m| < \rho\)
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\lambda\,\vek v)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek m)\,\lambda\,v_{\mathrm{i}} = \lambda \sum_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v)\,m_{\mathrm{i}} .\]
    With \(\vek m = h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) as in step 10 we get \(\vek g(\lambda\,\vek v) = \lambda\,\vek g(\vek v)\).
  4. A matrix. Let \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\) be the matrix with the entries \((\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = g_{\mathrm{i}}(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})/h\). Let \(|\vek v| < \rho\). By lemma 1.21, \(\vek v = v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The vectors \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) have the lengths \(|v_{\mathrm{x}}|\), \(|v_{\mathrm{y}}|\), \(|v_{\mathrm{z}}|\) and \(\sqrt{v_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + v_{\mathrm{y}}^2}\), which are not larger than \(|\vek v|\) (lemma 1.28) and are therefore smaller than \(\rho\). By step 10, used first for \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), then for \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek g(\vek v) = \vek g(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) + \vek g(v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) + \vek g(v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}})\). The vector \(v_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \((v_{\mathrm{j}}/h)\) times the vector \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) and has the length \(|v_{\mathrm{j}}| < \rho\), so by step 11, \(\vek g(v_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) = (v_{\mathrm{j}}/h)\,\vek g(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\). The component \(\ix{i}\) is
    \[g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek v) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{g_{\mathrm{i}}(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})}{h}\,v_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} (\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}}\,v_{\mathrm{j}} = (\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,\vek v)_{\mathrm{i}} .\]
  5. Antisymmetry. In (1.74) we put \(\vek v = h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\vek w = h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\). The vector \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) has only the component \(\ix{i}\) different from zero, and \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) only the component \(\ix{j}\), so of the sum on the left only the term with the component \(\ix{i}\) remains, and of the sum on the right only the term with the component \(\ix{j}\). The left side is \(h\,g_{\mathrm{i}}(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) = h^2\,(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the right side \(-h\,g_{\mathrm{j}}(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}) = -h^2\,(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ji}}\). So \((\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = -(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ji}}\), and \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\) is antisymmetric.

Let us draw steps 14 and 15 around the point \(C\) (figure 1.464). The grey dashed circle is the ball with radius \(\rho\) from step 5, in which \(\vek g(\vek v) = \mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,\vek v\) holds by step 12. The blue shaded disc with radius \(\rho/4\) around the point \(C\) is the set in which we will show that the gradient of displacements equals \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\). The point \(X\) lies in it. The grey dashed circle around \(X\) has radius \(\rho/4\). Its points are at a distance less than \(\rho/4 + \rho/4 = \rho/2\) from \(C\), so they lie in the ball with radius \(\rho\). A quarter is not necessary: every radius \(r\) with \(2r \le \rho\) will do. We take it because lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point is written with it. The blue step \(\Delta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) from \(X\) stays in the circle around \(X\), because \(|\Delta| < \rho/4\) (step 14). The blue step \(\Delta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\) from \(C\) stays in the blue disc (step 15).

  1. The gradient near \(C\). By step 12, \(\vek u(X) = \vek u(C) + \mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,\overrightarrow{CX}\) for every point \(X\) at a distance less than \(\rho\) from \(C\). Let \(X\) be at a distance less than \(\rho/4\) from \(C\). By lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point, all points at a distance less than \(\rho/4\) from \(X\) are at a distance less than \(\rho\) from \(C\). For \(0 < |\Delta| < \rho/4\) we therefore have, by lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix,
    \[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{i}}(X + \Delta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(X) &= \big(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,(\overrightarrow{CX} + \Delta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\big)_{\mathrm{i}} - \big(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\,\overrightarrow{CX}\big)_{\mathrm{i}} \\ &= \Delta\,(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}} . \end{aligned}\]
    The difference quotient is \((\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for every such \(\Delta\), so by lemma 1.26 on the limit of a number plus a multiple, \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}(X) = (\mat W_{\mathrm{C}})_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The displacement gradient equals \(\mat W_{\mathrm{C}}\) at all points at a distance less than \(\rho/4\) from \(C\).
  2. Zero derivatives of the gradient. By step 14 each function \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is constant at all points at a distance less than \(\rho/4\) from \(C\). For \(0 < |\Delta| < \rho/4\) we therefore have \(\big(H_{\mathrm{ij}}(C + \Delta\,\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}) - H_{\mathrm{ij}}(C)\big)/\Delta = 0\), and the partial derivative \(\partial H_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\) is zero at \(C\). We picked the point \(C\) arbitrarily, so each of the nine functions \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) has all partial derivatives equal to zero at every point of \(D\).
  3. A constant gradient. By lemma 1.133 on zero partial derivatives on a connected set, each function \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is constant on \(D\). We choose a point \(C_0\) of \(D\) and write \(\mat W = \mat H(C_0)\). By step 14 at \(X = C_0\), \(\mat W = \mat W_{\mathrm{C}_0}\), which is antisymmetric by step 13. So \(\mat H(P) = \mat W\) for every point \(P\) of \(D\).
  4. A shift. Let \(f_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) - \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\) for \(P\) in \(D\). The partial derivative of the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}\) with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(W_{\mathrm{ik}}\) (lemma 1.81), so \(\partial f_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}} = H_{\mathrm{ik}} - W_{\mathrm{ik}} = 0\) at every point of \(D\). By the same lemma on zero partial derivatives, each function \(f_{\mathrm{i}}\) is constant on \(D\). Let \(\vek a = (f_{\mathrm{x}}(C_0), f_{\mathrm{y}}(C_0), f_{\mathrm{z}}(C_0))\). Then \(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = f_{\mathrm{i}}(P) + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}(P) = a_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\), so \(\vek u(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) for every point \(P\) of \(D\).

2. The converse.

  1. The component \(\ix{i}\) of the field (1.72) is \(u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = a_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{ij}}\,x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\). The number \(a_{\mathrm{i}}\) has the derivative zero, and the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) has the derivative \(1\) with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(0\) with respect to the other coordinates (lemma 1.81). So \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = W_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at every point, and the displacement gradient is \(\mat W\).
  2. The small strain tensor is \(\tfrac12(\mat W + \mat W^\T)\). Since \(\mat W^\T = -\mat W\), this is \(\tfrac12(\mat W - \mat W) = \mat 0\).

Source: SADD (2.2.9) and (2.2.10) (PDF pp. 44-45) writes the most general small rigid-body displacement with components and says for the plane form (2.2.9) that it gives zero strains. That with zero strains the displacements are at most such a motion, SADD states without proof (§6.2, PDF p. 133). CM (PDF p. 143) shows that a displacement with a constant antisymmetric matrix is a small rigid rotation. The proof is not from the sources.

The proof had three parts, as announced, and each has its part of the figure. In steps 1 to 4 the derivative along a segment, together with the corollary on a function with zero derivative, showed that no segment in the body gets longer to first order. In steps 5 to 13 the triangle in the ball turned this perpendicularity into linearity: the equality (1.74), which swaps the roles of two vectors at the cost of a sign, gave the sum, the multiple and the antisymmetric matrix. In steps 14 to 17 we passed from the ball to the whole set, by broken lines, just as for the bar we concluded from a zero derivative that a function is constant on an interval. The proof needs no second derivatives. We will meet the derivative along a segment again in chapter 4, where we will also use the theorem.

Let us test the theorem on the square plate of section 1.17.6. Lengths are measured in centimetres, the side of the plate is \(5\), and the corners are \(O = (0, 0, 0)\), \(A = (5, 0, 0)\), \(B = (5, 5, 0)\) and \(C = (0, 5, 0)\). Take \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and the antisymmetric matrix with a single pair of entries, \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -s\) and \(W_{\mathrm{yx}} = s\), with \(s = 0{,}001\). The field is \(\vek u = \mat W\,\vek r = (-s\,y,\ s\,x,\ 0)\). In micrometres the side of the plate is \(5\ \text{cm} = 50\,000\) µm, and the corner \(A\) moves by \(s \cdot 50\,000\ \text{µm} = 0{,}001 \cdot 50\,000\ \text{µm} = 50\) µm. The displacements of the corners are

\[\vek u(A) = (0, 50, 0) , \qquad \vek u(B) = (-50, 50, 0) , \qquad \vek u(C) = (-50, 0, 0) .\]

Let us draw this (figure 1.465), seen from above. The axis \(x\) points to the right, the axis \(y\) up. The blackwhite square is the plate \(OABC\) before the movement. The movement is greatly magnified in the figure: instead of \(s = 0{,}001\), \(s = 0{,}3\) is drawn, so that it can be seen. The orange quadrilateral is the plate after the movement with the field \(\mat W\,\vek r\), with the corners \(A_1\), \(B_1\) and \(C_1\). It stays a square: the orange right-angle marks show a right angle at all four corners. The corner \(O\) does not move. The blue dimensions are the displacements of the corners \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\). Each is perpendicular to the segment from \(O\) to this corner: for \(A\) and \(C\) this is a side of the plate, for \(B\) the grey diagonal, as the grey right-angle marks show. Each is also \(s\) times the length of this segment, in the figure \(0{,}3 \cdot 5 = 1{,}5\) cm for \(A\) and \(C\) and \(0{,}3 \cdot 5\sqrt2 \approx 2{,}1\) cm for \(B\). So the plate turns about \(O\), and for such a large \(s\) it also grows slightly. The grey dashed square is the exact rotation with the same \(s\). Its lengths do not change, while the orange side is slightly longer, by a term with the square, as we computed at the start of the section.

Let us also write the vectors of the segments in micrometres, so that both factors in the sum (1.73) are in the same unit. For the segment \(OB\) with \(\vek d = (50\,000, 50\,000, 0)\) µm the sum is \((-50) \cdot 50\,000 + 50 \cdot 50\,000 + 0 = 0\) µm², and for the segment \(AC\) with \(\vek d = (-50\,000, 50\,000, 0)\) µm it is \((-50 - 0) \cdot (-50\,000) + (0 - 50) \cdot 50\,000 = 0\) µm². Each corner moves perpendicular to its segment from \(O\) (figure 1.465). The lengths, though, change by a term with a square. The segment \(OA\) of \(50\,000\) µm becomes the segment to the point \((50\,000, 50, 0)\) with the length

\[\sqrt{50\,000^2 + 50^2}\ \text{µm} = 50\,000{,}025\ \text{µm} ,\]

which is \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\) of the length more, the lengthening \(\sqrt{1 + s^2} - 1\) from the start of the section, written in micrometres. The exact rotation with the same \(s\) from section 1.17.6 moves the corner \(A\) to \((5c, 5s, 0)\), by \(5 \cdot (1 - c) = 2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-6}\) cm \(= 0{,}025\) µm less in the direction of the axis \(x\) than the field \(\mat W\vek r\) moves it. Both movements are rigid to first order, as the table at the start of the section shows, and they differ by a term with \(s^2\). For steel structures we are interested in strains around \(0{,}001\). The error \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\) is \(0{,}001 / (5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}) = 2000\) times smaller than that, so there the two rigid motions are equally good.

The theorem gives the answer to the question at the start of the section.

Corollary 1.135 Two fields with equal strains (polji z enakimi deformacijami)

Let \(D\) be a connected open set of points (definition 1.130), and let \(\vek u\) and \(\tilde{\vek u}\) be displacement fields, continuously differentiable on \(D\), that have the same small strain tensor at every point of \(D\). Then there are a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) such that

\[\tilde{\vek u}(P) = \vek u(P) + \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} \qquad \text{for every point } P \text{ of } D .\]
Proof

We must show that the difference of the fields satisfies the assumptions of theorem 1.134, item 1.

  1. Let \(\vek v = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\). The partial derivative of a difference is the difference of the partial derivatives (lemma 1.81), and the difference of continuous functions is continuous (corollary 1.69, item 1), so \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\).
  2. Entry \(\ix{i}\ix{j}\) of the small strain tensor of \(\vek v\) is \(\tfrac12\big(\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial v_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\). By step 1 it is the difference of the same entries for \(\tilde{\vek u}\) and \(\vek u\), which are equal by assumption. So the tensor of \(\vek v\) is zero at every point of \(D\).
  3. By theorem 1.134, item 1, \(\vek v(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) with a constant \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\), which is the claim.

Source: SADD (PDF p. 54), BOWER (PDF p. 61), BARBER §9.1.1 (PDF p. 139), where the claim is stated without proof: by integrating the strains we get the displacements only up to a rigid-body motion. The proof from the theorem is not from the sources.

So the displacement is determined by the strains up to six numbers: the three components of the vector \(\vek a\) and the three entries \(W_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{yz}}\) above the diagonal of the matrix \(\mat W\), since the entries below the diagonal are their opposites and the diagonal holds zeros (lemma 1.103, item 3). Six numbers are fixed by six conditions.

Let us look at this on the hanging bar. The steel hanging bar hangs under its own weight and is fixed in the model only at the centre \(O\) of the top face (the point \(O\) in figure 1.94, left). Its interior points form a cylinder, which is connected, so every other continuously differentiable field with the same strains differs from the field (1.18) at the interior points by an addition \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\). The fixing, however, is prescribed at the point \(O\), which lies on the surface, and the theorem speaks only about interior points. We therefore carry the relation from the interior to \(O\) along a sequence of points (figure 1.466, left).

On the left is the upper part of the bar, with the thickness magnified so that it can be seen. The point \(O\) is the centre of the top face, the axis \(x\) points downward. The blue dots are the interior points \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = (1/n, 0, 0)\) on the axis, with the coordinates in metres, for \(n = 1, 2, \dots\). As \(n\) grows, they approach the point \(O\), which is their limit. Now we need an assumption that we have not had so far. Both fields are to be continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the whole bar together with its surface. Without it the values of the field at \(O\) would not be connected with the values in the interior. With it the displacements and their partial derivatives are continuous at \(O\). The relation \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u + \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), which holds at every point \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\), therefore holds in the limit too, at the point \(O\) (lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points and lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence). The same holds for the partial derivatives of both fields. We need them because the fixing at \(O\) prescribes not only the displacement but also the rotation of the material, which is made of partial derivatives of the displacement.

What conditions does the fixing at \(O\) prescribe? The addition has at every point the displacement \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) and the small rotation tensor \(\mat W\), as we computed at the start of the section. At the point \(O\), where \(\vek r_{\mathrm{O}} = \vek 0\), it moves the material by \(\vek a\) and turns it by \(\mat W\). A fixing that holds back only the displacement of the point \(O\) requires \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and leaves \(\mat W\) arbitrary. Let us draw what this allows (figure 1.466, right). The bar is fixed at the point \(O\). The orange bar is the same bar, rotated about \(O\) by the angle, which is greatly magnified. The displacement of the point \(O\) is zero in both, so a fixing that holds back only the displacement does not tell them apart. A rotation does not change the strains, and the displacement of the bar would not be determined. For it to be determined, the fixing at \(O\) must prevent the turning of the material as well. CM prescribes such an idealized fixing: the displacement at \(O\) is zero and the material next to \(O\) does not turn (CM (7.3.16) and PDF p. 306). The field of the bar satisfies both conditions. The displacement is \(\vek u(O) = \vek 0\), and we compute the entries of the small rotation tensor from (1.18), as \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) before the lemma on the derivatives of the rotation:

\[\begin{aligned} \omega_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) = \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y - 0{,}6\,a\,y) = -0{,}6\,a\,y , \\ \omega_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) = \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,z - 0{,}6\,a\,z) = -0{,}6\,a\,z , \\ \omega_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\Big) = \tfrac12\,(0 - 0) = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) does not contain \(z\), the component \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) does not contain \(y\), so the last derivatives are zero. At \(y = z = 0\) all three are zero. An addition that does not spoil the conditions must have \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and \(\mat W = \mat 0\). The field of the bar is therefore the only field with these strains that satisfies the conditions. CM writes the second condition so that all partial derivatives of the displacement off the diagonal of the gradient are zero at \(O\), which for the bar, which has no shear strains at \(O\), means the same.

The theorem and the corollary only require the body to be connected, not to be free of holes. The ring is connected by lemma 1.131, so two displacement fields of the ring with the same strains are equal up to \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\), although the ring has a hole. For the two separate cubes of figure 1.453, though, the corollary does not hold, because the set is not connected. The corollary is about how many fields with given strains there are when there is one. Whether there is one is another question, and for the ring the answer will be different. We look at this in the next section.

1.18.5 Bodies with holes

Theorem 1.127 says that strains that come from a displacement field satisfy the compatibility equations. So the equations are a necessary condition: if they fail, there is no displacement field. But are they also a sufficient condition? Does a displacement field exist for every six functions that satisfy the equations? The answer depends on the shape of the body. Let us draw two bodies (figure 1.467).

On the left is a body without a hole, on the right a ring, a body with a hole. At the end of the section we will write for the ring six functions that satisfy the compatibility equations at every point of the ring, and the whole ring has no displacement field with these strains.

How would we find the displacement from the strains? We pick a point \(P\) and the displacement there, for example zero. We get the displacement at another point \(Q\) by walking from \(P\) to \(Q\) along some curve in the body and adding up the changes of the displacement over short steps. By theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step, the change over a short step is almost exactly the sum of the products of the partial derivatives with the components of the step. The partial derivatives of the displacement are not only strains, though: they also contain the rotation of the material (definition 1.116). So the rotation too has to be obtained by adding up its changes along the path, and these changes are determined by derivatives of the strains (lemma 1.128 on derivatives of the rotation from derivatives of the strains, SADD (2.6.3)-(2.6.7), PDF p. 52). Exact adding up along a curve we meet only in section 3.5. But already now we can see where the compatibility equations enter this computation and why a hole spoils everything. Let us take a plane problem, where \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) depend only on \(x\) and \(y\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and in it the rotation \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) (figure 1.468).

  1. What the strains prescribe. By lemma 1.128 with \(\ix{i} = x\), \(\ix{j} = y\) and \(\ix{k} = x\) or \(\ix{k} = y\), the partial derivatives of the rotation must be
    \[\frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x} = p , \quad p = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x} , \qquad \frac{\partial\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} = q , \quad q = \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x} .\]
    We know the functions \(p\) and \(q\) once we know the strains. We look for a function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) with these two partial derivatives.
  2. A small loop. We go around the rectangle in the body with the corner \(A = (x_{\mathrm{A}}, y_{\mathrm{A}})\) and sides \(s\) and \(t\) in the directions of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), counterclockwise. In the figure, in part (1), the loop is drawn as four blue arrows just inside the sides: at the bottom to the right, on the right upward, at the top to the left and on the left downward. Beside each is the estimate of the change on that side. There is a minus at the top and left sides, because we walk them in the direction opposite to the axis, so with a step of negative sign. We estimate the change of the rotation along each side as for a short step: by the value of the prescribed derivative at the middle of the side, multiplied by the length of the side and by the sign of the direction of walking. The sum of these estimates around the loop is
    \[Z(s, t) = p(M_1)\,s + q(M_2)\,t - p(M_3)\,s - q(M_4)\,t ,\]
    where \(M_1 = (x_{\mathrm{A}} + \tfrac s2, y_{\mathrm{A}})\) is the middle of the bottom side, \(M_2 = (x_{\mathrm{A}} + s, y_{\mathrm{A}} + \tfrac t2)\) of the right one, \(M_3 = (x_{\mathrm{A}} + \tfrac s2, y_{\mathrm{A}} + t)\) of the top one and \(M_4 = (x_{\mathrm{A}}, y_{\mathrm{A}} + \tfrac t2)\) of the left one.
  3. The mean value theorem. We chose the middles of the sides because then the points \(M_1\) and \(M_3\) lie on the same vertical segment, and the points \(M_4\) and \(M_2\) on the same horizontal one. We apply the mean value theorem 1.84 to \(p\) along the vertical segment and to \(q\) along the horizontal one, as in steps 3 and 4 of the proof of theorem 1.125. We get a point \(T_1\) between \(M_1\) and \(M_3\) and a point \(T_2\) between \(M_4\) and \(M_2\) such that \(p(M_3) - p(M_1) = t\,\partial p / \partial y\,(T_1)\) and \(q(M_2) - q(M_4) = s\,\partial q / \partial x\,(T_2)\). Therefore
    \[Z(s, t) = s\,t\,\Big(\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}(T_2) - \frac{\partial p}{\partial y}(T_1)\Big) .\]
    This is the same structure as for the double difference (1.66): the difference of values on opposite sides becomes a derivative at an intermediate point.
  4. The compatibility equation. We differentiate \(q\) with respect to \(x\) and \(p\) with respect to \(y\) (lemma 1.81), and the mixed derivatives of the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are equal by theorem 1.125:
    \[\frac{\partial q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial p}{\partial y} = 2\,\frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}}{\partial x\,\partial y} - \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial y^2} - \frac{\partial^2 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\partial x^2} .\]
    The right side is the right side of the first equation (1.68) minus its left side. So the first equation holds exactly when \(\partial q / \partial x = \partial p / \partial y\). This is the condition that, by theorem 1.125, every function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) whose partial derivatives \(p\) and \(q\) are continuously differentiable satisfies.
  5. What this means for the loop. The step has two claims. The first is new: if the first equation holds at every point, the sum of the estimates around a small loop is small even compared with the area that the loop encloses. Step 7 will need this, as it will add up the loops of many small squares. The second repeats theorem 1.127, only for the rotation instead of the displacement: if the equation does not hold, the function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) does not exist. In doing so it shows where in the loop this is seen. First the first claim. If the first equation holds at every point, the bracket in step 3 equals \(\partial p / \partial y\,(T_2) - \partial p / \partial y\,(T_1)\). When we shrink the rectangle towards \(A\), \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) approach \(A\), and when \(\partial p / \partial y\) is continuous, the bracket approaches zero. The sum of the estimates around the loop is then small even compared with the area \(s\,t\) that the loop encloses. Now the second. If the first equation does not hold at \(A\), the quotient \(Z(s, t)/(s\,t) = \partial q/\partial x\,(T_2) - \partial p/\partial y\,(T_1)\) approaches the difference \(\partial q/\partial x\,(A) - \partial p/\partial y\,(A)\), which by step 4 is not zero. Why then is there no function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\)? Suppose it exists. When we go around the rectangle, we return to \(A\), so the sum of the true changes of \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) along the four sides is zero. The estimate \(Z(s, t)\) differs from this sum by the error \(Z(s, t) - 0\), which we compute with the double difference \(g(s, t)\) of the function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) ((1.66)). The true changes on the bottom and top sides give together \(-g(s, t)\), the true changes on the right and left sides give \(g(s, t)\). Steps 4 to 7 of the proof of theorem 1.125, applied to \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) with the partial derivatives \(p\) and \(q\), give the points \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) in the rectangle such that \(g(s, t) = s\,t\,\partial q/\partial x\,(Q_1) = s\,t\,\partial p/\partial y\,(Q_2)\). With step 3 the error is therefore
    \[\begin{aligned} Z(s, t) - 0 &= \Big(-s\,t\,\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}(T_1) + g(s, t)\Big) + \Big(s\,t\,\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}(T_2) - g(s, t)\Big) \\ &= s\,t\,\Big(\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}(Q_2) - \frac{\partial p}{\partial y}(T_1)\Big) + s\,t\,\Big(\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}(T_2) - \frac{\partial q}{\partial x}(Q_1)\Big) . \end{aligned}\]
    When the strains have continuous second partial derivatives, the derivatives \(\partial p/\partial y\) and \(\partial q/\partial x\) are continuous at \(A\). For every error \(\eta > 0\) there is therefore a \(\delta > 0\) such that their values at the points at distance less than \(\delta\) from \(A\) differ from the values at \(A\) by less than \(\eta/4\). For \(s^2 + t^2 < \delta^2\) all four points \(T_1\), \(T_2\), \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are such, since they lie in the rectangle (step 1 of the proof of theorem 1.125). By the triangle inequality (lemma 1.6) each bracket is then smaller in size than \(\eta/2\), so \(|Z(s, t)| < \eta\,s\,t\). The error of the estimate is therefore small even compared with the area \(s\,t\). For the same \(s\) and \(t\) the quotient \(Z(s, t)/(s\,t)\) differs from the difference \(\partial q/\partial x\,(A) - \partial p/\partial y\,(A)\) by less than \(\eta/4 + \eta/4 = \eta/2\). By the triangle inequality this difference is therefore smaller in size than \(\eta + \eta/2\) for every \(\eta > 0\), that is, than every positive number, and by lemma 1.34 on inequalities with all positive numbers it is zero. The first equation would therefore hold at \(A\). If it does not hold, the function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) does not exist. Take the first strip from section 1.18.1, with the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), where \(k = -10\ \text{m}^{-2}\). For it \(p = 2k\,y\) and \(q = 0\), so \(\partial p/\partial y = 2k\) and \(\partial q/\partial x = 0\) at every point. Both brackets in the error are zero: if \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) existed, the estimate would be exact, \(Z(s, t) = 0\). By step 3, however,
    \[Z(s, t) = s\,t\,(0 - 2k) = -2k\,s\,t ,\]
    for \(k = -10\ \text{m}^{-2}\) and \(s = t = 1\) mm is therefore \(-2 \cdot (-10\ \text{m}^{-2}) \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 = 2 \cdot 10^{-5}\). The estimate is \(-2k\) times the area of the loop, while the error would be zero. The estimate of the change of the rotation after going around a square with edge 1 mm is not zero, but the true change would have to be zero. The function \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) therefore does not exist, and the pieces of the strip do not fit together.
  6. From the rotation to the displacement. When \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) exists, we know all partial derivatives of the displacement, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and we look for the displacement in the same way. The condition from step 4 is satisfied for it by itself. By lemma 1.128, item 2, we have \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{i}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{k}} + \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ik}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{j}} - \partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}} / \partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the right side does not change when we swap \(\ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k}\), because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jk}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{kj}}\). So no new equation arises.
  7. From loops to paths. Let us also draw part (2) of the figure. The closed thick line is the boundary of a body without a hole, the point \(P\) is the start of the paths, the point \(Q\) the end. The paths go along the sides of a grid of small squares: the lower, blackwhite one first to the right and then upward, the upper, blue one first upward, then to the right and at the end downward to \(Q\). The grey squares of the grid between the paths lie in the body, and this is the only thing that we require of the two paths. The two thin blackwhite loops in two neighbouring squares show with arrows beside each side that we go around each counterclockwise. Let us add up the sums \(Z\) around the loops of all the squares between the paths. Every inner side, like the common side of two neighbouring squares, is traversed by the neighbouring squares in opposite directions. Both estimate its change with the same value of the prescribed derivative at its middle, multiplied by the same length, only with opposite signs, so the estimates cancel. Only the sides of the two paths remain, and the sum is exactly the sum of the estimates along the lower path minus the sum along the upper one. By step 5 each term is small compared with the area of its square, so the difference of the two paths is small compared with the area between the paths, and on an ever finer grid it approaches zero. So we get the same rotation along both paths, and then by step 6 the same displacement.

Steps 1 to 6 are proved with the tools of this chapter. Step 7 is only a sketch: exactly, with true sums instead of estimates and for arbitrary paths, we prove it in chapter 4, section 4.7.9. The sketch says what BARBER states (PDF p. 46): if the path from \(P\) to \(Q\) can be turned into every other path between the same two points by small changes, we get the same displacement along all paths, and a displacement field exists. In space the rotation has three components, \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\), and a loop can be placed in each of the three planes. The same computation as in steps 1 to 4 gives nine conditions, one for each of the three components of the rotation and each of the three planes of the loop. Let us write which equation (1.68) gives which (we checked the computation with SymPy):

component of the rotation loop in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) loop in the plane \(x\)-\(z\) loop in the plane \(y\)-\(z\)
\(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) equation 1 equation 4 equation 5
\(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) equation 4 equation 3 equation 6
\(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\) equation 5 equation 6 equation 2

The nine conditions are therefore exactly six different equations (1.68), since equations 4, 5 and 6 appear twice in the table.

Figure 1.467 compares two bodies. On the left is the body without a hole, the blackwhite closed line is its boundary. The blue closed curve lies in it. The two smaller grey dashed copies and the dot show that the curve gradually shrinks to a point without leaving the body. On the right is the ring, a body with a hole between the outer and the inner blackwhite circle, with the points \(P\) and \(Q\) on each side of the hole. The grey dashed circle around the hole is a closed curve that we cannot shrink to a point without leaving the ring. In a ring, however, the path above the hole cannot be turned into the path below it without passing through the hole, that is, outside the body (figure 1.467). Between the paths there is no grid of squares that would all lie in the body, because the hole lies in between, where the strains are not defined. Step 7 therefore does not hold there, and the displacement obtained along one path can differ from the displacement obtained along the other.

A body with a hole differs from a body without one in something else too. So far every point of the body had a single displacement. In a body with a hole, however, a point can get two different displacements, depending on which side we look at it from. Love describes such a case on a hollow cylinder (LOVE, PDF p. 240), which we draw along the axis (figure 1.469).

In part (1) the blackwhite circles are the inner and outer edge of the cylinder, the point \(O\) is the axis. From the cylinder we cut out a narrow wedge between two planes through the axis, in grey in the figure, and greatly enlarged so that it can be seen. The blackwhite radial lines are the faces of the cut. The body before the joining is therefore the cylinder without the wedge. In part (2) we bring the faces together and join them along the thick orange line. The orange circles are the cylinder after the joining, its shape is only illustrative. The grey dashed lines show where the faces were before the joining. The wedge is narrow, so after the joining the body takes almost the same region as the hollow cylinder before the cut, and we write the displacement as a function of the point of this hollow cylinder. The points \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) on the opposite faces of the cut, in part (2) the grey dots at the positions of the faces before the joining, move to the same point \(S\) of the joint, each with its own displacement: \(S_1\) by \(\overrightarrow{S_1 S}\), \(S_2\) by \(\overrightarrow{S_2 S}\). The point \(S\) therefore has two displacements, depending on whether we look at it from the side of \(S_1\) or of \(S_2\). They differ by \(\overrightarrow{S_1 S} - \overrightarrow{S_2 S} = \overrightarrow{S_1 S_2}\), the vector from \(S_1\) to \(S_2\) across the wedge. If we go along a path around the axis, we return to the same point, but the displacement on returning is not equal to the displacement at the start, because we went across the joint, where the material moved so that the two faces coincided (LOVE, PDF p. 240). The pieces of the cylinder therefore stay stretched or compressed after the joining, although no external force acts on the cylinder. The region with a hole is turned by a cut into a region without a hole, and the displacement may jump across the cut (LOVE, PDF p. 241).

From history

Let us draw a timeline. The axis shows years. That the displacement may fail to be a single-valued function of the point was first indicated by G. Weingarten in 1901. Two-dimensional bodies, such as a plane circular ring, were treated by A. Timpe in 1906. A more general theory was developed in a series of notes by Vito Volterra, who called such deformations distorsioni. Love calls them dislocations (dislokacije) (LOVE, PDF p. 240). Volterra published a comprehensive account in 1907 (LOVE, PDF p. 240, TIMO, PDF p. 345).

The property that separates a body without a hole, such as a solid cylinder, from a body with a hole, such as a ring, has its own name. Let us describe it first with a rubber band (figure 1.471).

On the right the blackwhite closed line is the outline of the region \(D\). The blue line is a rubber band stretched in \(D\), a line that ends where it starts. We denote it by \(\gamma\). The blue dot \(\gamma(0)\) is its start and at the same time its end. We gradually squeeze the rubber band. The two grey lines inside it are its positions after a third and after two thirds of the time, and the point \(Z\) is the point to which we squeeze it at the end. The grey dashed line is the path that the point \(\gamma(0)\) makes in the process. It is short because \(Z\) is near.

On the left we write all this with numbers. The axes are \(s\) and \(t\). The number \(s\) from \(0\) to \(1\) says where on the rubber band we are, and the number \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\) says how much of the shrinking time has passed. The square with the end values \(0\) and \(1\) beside the axes consists of all pairs \((s, t)\). The arrow \(H\) says that the rule \(H\) assigns to every pair \((s, t)\) a point \(H(s, t)\) in \(D\): this is where, at time \(t\), the point of the rubber band that was at \(s\) at the start arrives. The bottom side, blue, at \(t = 0\), is the rubber band at the start. The horizontal grey lines at \(t = 1/3\) and \(t = 2/3\) are the rubber band at these times. The top side at \(t = 1\) goes entirely to the point \(Z\). The left and right edge, grey dashed, are \(s = 0\) and \(s = 1\), the start and end of the rubber band, which are the same point. Both therefore go to the same grey dashed path on the right, which we write as \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\).

Definition 1.136 Simply connected body (enostavno povezano telo)

Let \(D\) be a set of points of space.

  1. A closed curve (sklenjena krivulja) in \(D\) is a rule \(\gamma\) whose input is a number \(s\) from the interval \([0, 1]\) and whose output is a point \(\gamma(s)\) of \(D\), such that every coordinate of the point \(\gamma(s)\) is a continuous function of the number \(s\) on \([0, 1]\) (definition 1.58) and \(\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)\).
  2. A closed curve \(\gamma\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\) if there is a rule \(H\) whose input is a point \((s, t)\) of the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) and whose output is a point \(H(s, t)\) of \(D\), such that every coordinate of the point \(H(s, t)\) is a continuous function of the point \((s, t)\) of the square (definition 1.67, written for points of the plane), and such that \(H(s, 0) = \gamma(s)\) for every \(s\), \(H(s, 1)\) is the same point for all \(s\) and \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\) for every \(t\).
  3. The set \(D\) is simply connected (enostavno povezana) if every closed curve in \(D\) can be shrunk continuously to a point in \(D\). A body is simply connected if the set of its interior points is simply connected. A set or a body that is not simply connected is multiply connected (večkratno povezana), like the ring.

Source: SADD §2.6 (PDF p. 53), KREYSZIG §10.2 (PDF p. 449), where the definition is given in words. The formulation with the rule \(H\) is not from these sources.

The definition writes precisely what we described with a rubber band. As \(s\) runs from \(0\) to \(1\), the point \(\gamma(s)\) runs along the whole line and returns to the starting point. Continuity of the coordinates means that the line has no jumps. For every fixed \(t\) the rule \(s \mapsto H(s, t)\) is again a closed curve, since \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\): this is the rubber band at time \(t\). All points \(H(s, t)\) lie in \(D\), so the rubber band does not leave the set while it shrinks. The coordinates are continuous functions of the point \((s, t)\), so the rubber band neither tears nor jumps, neither along the line nor in time. For a body we look at the interior points, because the strains and their derivatives are defined there. The definition is written for sets of points of space, and for sets in the plane it reads the same. LEBL2 (PDF p. 86) describes a simply connected domain as a connected open set in which every path between two points can be continuously deformed into every other path between the same two points, and KREYSZIG (PDF p. 449) writes the definition for domains. We require connectedness separately in the theorems (definition 1.130).

A cube, a cylinder and a ball are simply connected: we shrink a curve by moving each of its points at the same time along a segment towards one chosen point \(Z\). In coordinates the rule is

\[H(s, t) = (1 - t)\,\gamma(s) + t\,Z .\]

At \(t = 0\) we have \(H(s, 0) = \gamma(s)\), at \(t = 1\) we have \(H(s, 1) = Z\), and since \(\gamma(0) = \gamma(1)\), we have \(H(0, t) = H(1, t)\). The point \(H(s, t)\) lies on the segment from \(\gamma(s)\) to \(Z\), so it is in the body whenever this whole segment lies in the body. This is also how figure 1.471 is drawn: the intermediate positions are reduced copies of the curve toward \(Z\), and the path of the point \(\gamma(0)\) is straight. We prove this precisely in chapter 4, section 4.7.8, for all bodies in which every point can be joined to a chosen point by a straight segment inside the body.

A body with a cavity is not necessarily multiply connected. A cylinder with a spherical cavity inside is simply connected, because every curve around the cavity can be slid past it (SADD, PDF p. 53), and so is a thick spherical shell, the body between two spheres with a common centre (KREYSZIG, PDF p. 449). Let us draw why (figure 1.472).

On the left is the cylinder, and in its interior a spherical cavity, an empty space that the material surrounds on all sides. The blue rubber band \(\gamma\) embraces the cavity around its equator. Behind, where the cavity hides it, it is dashed. We can slide the rubber band upward along a sphere slightly larger than the cavity, so it stays in the material all the time. Above the cavity it shrinks to the point \(Z\). On the right is the tube, through which the hole goes from the top to the bottom face, its hidden walls dashed. The rubber band around the hole can slide upward only as far as the top face. To shrink, it would have to go across the hole or past the top face, both times out of the body. A hole or a cavity makes a body multiply connected exactly when there is in the body a closed curve around it that we cannot shrink, as with the tube and the ring. A spherical cavity does not do this. That the cylinder with such a cavity and the spherical shell are simply connected, we prove in the same section of chapter 4. A ring, however, is not simply connected, because a curve around the hole cannot be shrunk without passing through the hole (SADD, PDF p. 53, likewise KREYSZIG, PDF p. 449, for the interior of a torus). We prove this too in the same section, for the ring with radii 40 mm and 60 mm and any height, hence also for such a tube, which is only a tall ring. If we cut a ring, it becomes simply connected, which we prove there as well.

Theorem 1.137 Sufficiency of the compatibility equations (zadostnost enačb kompatibilnosti)

Let the set of interior points of a body be connected (definition 1.130) and simply connected, and let six functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) be defined at the interior points of the body, with continuous partial derivatives of first and second order. If they satisfy the compatibility equations (1.68) at every interior point, they are compatible strains: there is a displacement field from which we get them by (1.63).

Source: SADD §2.6 (PDF pp. 52-53), CM §3.7.2 (PDF p. 151). We prove the theorem in full in chapter 4, section 4.7.9. SADD proves it by adding up changes of the displacement along a curve and with a theorem about such sums around closed curves (Stokes' theorem), without stating the smoothness requirements separately. Continuous derivatives up to second order are what his proof uses of the strains.

We prove the theorem in chapter 4, once we can add up small changes precisely (section 3.5). First, in section 4.7.7, we prove it for bodies in which every point can be joined to one chosen point by a straight segment that does not leave the body. The box, the cylinder and the ball are such bodies, the ring is not. Then, in section 4.7.9, we build paths from several segments that avoid the holes, and with simple connectedness we show that the result does not depend on the choice of the path. The books make this step with Stokes' theorem about sums around closed curves (SADD, PDF p. 53), but we will manage with straight segments in small balls. The displacement is determined by the strains up to a rigid-body displacement: in a connected body two fields with the same strains differ only by a shift and a small rotation of the body as a whole, \(\vek a + \mat W\vek r\) (corollary 1.135 on two fields with equal strains, SADD, PDF p. 54). This agrees with what we saw in section 1.6: a rigid-body displacement does not change distances, so it does not change the strains.

Why the body has to be simply connected is shown by an example (figure 1.458). A thin ring with an inner radius of 40 mm and an outer radius of 60 mm, the ring of lemma 1.131 with a small height \(2c\), lies in the plane \(z = 0\), with its centre at the origin \(O\). Let us prescribe to it a strain and write it on the board (figure 1.473). The example is not from a source, but it follows the idea of BARBER §2.2.1 (PDF pp. 47-48).

The ring with the centre \(O\) is drawn from above, with the axes \(x\) and \(y\). At a point \(P = (x, y, z)\) of the ring, which is at the distance \(\rho = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) from the axis \(z\), we draw two directions. The unit vector \(\vek e = (-y, x, 0)/\rho\) points along the ring, around the hole, and touches the circle through \(P\). The unit vector \(\vek n = (x, y, 0)/\rho\) points away from the centre. The sum of the products of their components is \((-y\,x + x\,y)/\rho^2 = 0\), so they are perpendicular, as the grey right-angle mark shows. The prescribed strain says:

  • every short fibre in the direction \(\vek e\), along the ring, shortens by a thousandth, \(\varepsilon(\vek e) = -0{,}001\),
  • every short fibre in the direction \(\vek n\), toward the centre, keeps its length, \(\varepsilon(\vek n) = 0\),
  • the right angle between these two fibres stays right.

In the axes \(x\) and \(y\) the components that correspond to it are

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= -0{,}001\,\frac{y^2}{\rho^2} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -0{,}001\,\frac{x^2}{\rho^2} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &= 0{,}001\,\frac{x\,y}{\rho^2} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

Let us check them first at the point \(Q = (0, 50, 0)\) on the axis \(y\), with lengths in millimetres. There \(\vek e\) points in the direction \(-x\), \(\vek n\) in the direction \(y\), and the components are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -0{,}001\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). The fibre along the axis \(x\) shortens by a thousandth, the fibre along the axis \(y\) keeps its length, and the right angle between them stays right, exactly as prescribed. At a general point \(P\) the double sum (1.53) with \(\vek e = (-y, x, 0)/\rho\) gives

\[\varepsilon(\vek e) \approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\frac{y^2}{\rho^2} - 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\frac{x\,y}{\rho^2} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\frac{x^2}{\rho^2} = -0{,}001\,\frac{y^4 + 2x^2 y^2 + x^4}{\rho^4} = -0{,}001 ,\]

and with \(\vek n = (x, y, 0)/\rho\) it likewise gives \(-0{,}001\,(x^2 y^2 - 2x^2 y^2 + x^2 y^2)/\rho^4 = 0\). That the right angle stays right at every point too, we show in chapter 4, where we write the components in rotated axes.

What happens to the ring is drawn in figure 1.458.

Let us draw the ring before the deformation (figure 1.458, left). The blackwhite circles with radii 40 mm and 60 mm are the inner and outer edge. Between them is one more circle, with radius 50 mm, and segments every \(45^\circ\) point toward the centre. At the place of the eighth segment, at \(0^\circ\), is the cut. We draw the circles and segments because the prescribed deformation speaks about fibres along circles and fibres toward the centre. The point \(O\) is the centre. We first cut the ring along a segment from the inner to the outer edge (figure 1.458, left). The cut ring is simply connected (the proof is in chapter 4, section 4.7.8). It takes the prescribed strain like this. Every circle around the centre keeps its radius, and its arc shortens by a thousandth, like a fan that we close a little. The segments pointing toward the centre only turn about the centre. Their length stays the same, and they stay perpendicular to the circles, since a radius is always perpendicular to its circle. So the cut ring takes the prescribed strain. That the cut ring really has a displacement field whose small strain tensor is exactly the prescribed one, we only state here. We prove it in chapter 4, section 4.7.9, and everything that follows about the ring rests on it. The ends of the cut, though, move apart (figure 1.458, right). A circle of radius \(r\) has the circumference \(2\pi r\), so its arc shortens by \(0{,}001 \cdot 2\pi r\), and by that much the ends of the cut move apart on this circle. On the inner edge this is \(0{,}001 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 40\) mm \(= 0{,}251\) mm, on the outer edge \(0{,}001 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 60\) mm \(= 0{,}377\) mm. The gap is wider outside than inside, in proportion to the radius, so it has the shape of a wedge. One end of the cut is turned about the centre relative to the other.

In the middle of the figure the neighbourhood of the point \(S\) is enlarged. The small grey dashed circle just around \(S\) on the left marks where this neighbourhood is, and the large one in the middle is a circle with radius \(2{,}5\) mm around \(S\). In the middle are the cut and the point \(S\) on it. The points \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+\) are above the cut, the points \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-\) below it, at the distance \(1/n\) mm from \(S\), for \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4\). Only \(S_1^\pm\) and \(S_2^\pm\) are labelled, the smaller dots closer to \(S\) are \(S_3^\pm\) and \(S_4^\pm\). The arrows point toward \(S\), because we approach \(S\). On the right is the cut ring after the deformation, in orange, with the upper and lower end of the cut. Across the gap are three dimensions. The grey dimensions at the radii \(43\) and \(57\) mm show that the gap is wider outside. The blue dimension is the gap between the ends on the circle with radius \(50\) mm, to which the points just above the cut and just below it move. The shortening is greatly magnified: \(0{,}08\) instead of \(0{,}001\), so the gap in the drawing is about 25 mm instead of \(0{,}314\) mm.

Since the cut ring has a displacement field, by theorem 1.127 the prescribed strains satisfy the compatibility equations at every interior point of the cut ring. We could have made the cut anywhere, and the strain would be the same, because the prescription around the centre is the same everywhere: at every point the fibre along the ring shortens by a thousandth and the fibre toward the centre keeps its length. So the equations hold at every point of the ring. We see this directly from the components too. We check the first equation (1.68) on the board, with \(\rho^2 = x^2 + y^2\) and \(c = -0{,}001\). The components are

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c\,\frac{y^2}{\rho^2} = c\left(1 - \frac{x^2}{\rho^2}\right) , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = c\,\frac{x^2}{\rho^2} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = -c\,\frac{x\,y}{\rho^2} .\]

After division by \(c\) the equation \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx},\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy},\mathrm{xx}} = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{xy}}\) becomes \(-f_{\mathrm{yy}} + f_{\mathrm{xx}} = -2\,h_{\mathrm{xy}}\), with \(f = x^2/\rho^2\) and \(h = x\,y/\rho^2\), since the constant \(c\) gives zero when differentiated. We differentiate one derivative per display:

\[f_{\mathrm{y}} = -\frac{2x^2 y}{\rho^4} , \qquad f_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\frac{2x^2\,(x^2 - 3y^2)}{\rho^6} = \frac{-2x^4 + 6x^2 y^2}{\rho^6} ,\]
\[f_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{2x\,y^2}{\rho^4} , \qquad f_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\frac{2y^2\,(3x^2 - y^2)}{\rho^6} = \frac{-6x^2 y^2 + 2y^4}{\rho^6} ,\]
\[h_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{y\,(y^2 - x^2)}{\rho^4} , \qquad h_{\mathrm{xy}} = \frac{-x^4 + 6x^2 y^2 - y^4}{\rho^6} .\]

We substitute: the left side is \(f_{\mathrm{xx}} - f_{\mathrm{yy}} = (2x^4 - 12x^2 y^2 + 2y^4)/\rho^6\), the right side \(-2\,h_{\mathrm{xy}} = (2x^4 - 12x^2 y^2 + 2y^4)/\rho^6\). The sides are equal at every point with \(\rho \neq 0\), so at every point of the ring (we also checked every derivative with SymPy). The other five hold because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero and no component depends on \(z\), so all their terms are zero. Can the whole ring take these strains too? Let us show by contradiction that it cannot. We denote by \(\vek u\) the displacement field of the cut ring that opens the gap, and suppose that the whole ring also has a continuously differentiable displacement field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) with the prescribed strains.

  1. The cut ring is a part of the ring, so \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is defined at its points too. The cut ring is an open set (lemma 1.131), so the partial derivatives of \(\tilde{\vek u}\) at its points are the same whether we look at the whole ring or only at the cut one. The field \(\tilde{\vek u}\), looked at only at the points of the cut ring, is therefore a continuously differentiable displacement field of the cut ring with the same strains as \(\vek u\).
  2. The cut ring is connected (lemma 1.131). By corollary 1.135 on fields with equal strains there are therefore a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) such that \(\tilde{\vek u}(P) = \vek u(P) + \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) at every point \(P\) of the cut ring (SADD, PDF p. 54).
  3. Let us choose the point \(S = (50, 0, 0)\) on the cut, with lengths in millimetres (figure 1.458, enlarged in the middle). We approach it from above through the points \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+ = (50, 1/n, 0)\) and from below through the points \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^- = (50, -1/n, 0)\), \(n = 1, 2, \dots\) All these points are in the cut ring, since their coordinate \(y\) is different from zero, and both sequences converge to \(S\), since their terms are at distance \(1/n\) from \(S\).
  4. The field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is continuously differentiable on the ring, which contains \(S\) too, so it is continuous at \(S\) (lemma 1.91). By lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points, \(\tilde{\vek u}(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+)\) and \(\tilde{\vek u}(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-)\) therefore approach the same vector \(\tilde{\vek u}(S)\). The components of the field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) are polynomials and are continuous (corollary 1.69), so \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) too approaches the same vector \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{S}}\) along both sequences.
  5. By step 2, \(\vek u = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek a - \mat W\,\vek r\) at the points of both sequences. By step 4 and lemma 1.60 on computing with limits of sequences, applied to each component, the difference \(\vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+) - \vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-)\) approaches \(\vek 0\).

Why is the gap between the ends of the cut exactly the difference of the displacements? Let us draw the neighbourhood of the point \(S\) before the deformation and after it (figure 1.474). The thick grey line is the cut before the deformation, the point \(S\) lies on it. The point \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+\) just above the cut and the point \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-\) just below it are only \(2/n\) mm apart before the deformation. After the deformation the upper end of the cut is the upper orange line, the lower end the lower one, both rotated about the centre of the ring. The point \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+\) moves by the displacement \(\vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+)\) to the position \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+ + \vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+)\), the point \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-\) by the displacement \(\vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-)\) to the position \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^- + \vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-)\). The positions after the deformation differ by

\[\big(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+ + \vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+)\big) - \big(S_{\mathrm{n}}^- + \vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-)\big) = \overrightarrow{S_{\mathrm{n}}^- S_{\mathrm{n}}^+} + \vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+) - \vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-) .\]

The first part is \(2/n\) mm long and goes to zero. What remains is the difference of the displacements, and its limit is the gap between the ends of the cut at \(S\). Two points that were together at \(S\) before the deformation are apart after it by as much as their displacements differ.

  1. The field \(\vek u\) of the cut ring, however, jumps across the cut. The displacements of the points \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+\) and \(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-\) approach the displacements of the upper and lower end of the cut at \(S\). This is a property of the field \(\vek u\), which we prove in chapter 4 together with its existence (section 4.7.9), and here we take it as given. By figure 1.474 the limit of the difference \(\vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^+) - \vek u(S_{\mathrm{n}}^-)\) is the gap between the ends on the circle with radius \(50\) mm, \(0{,}001 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 50\) mm \(= 0{,}314\) mm. The difference therefore approaches a vector of length \(0{,}314\) mm, not the vector \(\vek 0\). This contradicts step 5.

The field \(\vek a + \mat W\vek r\) that the corollary allows is continuous across the cut as well, so it does not change the difference between the displacements of the two ends of the cut, and the gap in figure 1.458 cannot close. The whole ring cannot take these strains, even though the compatibility equations hold at every one of its points.

If we cut such a ring, strained it and forced the ends of the cut together, the pieces would have to strain further so that the ends meet. Displacement fields with a jump across a cut are used for cracks and for dislocations, defects in the structure of metal crystals (SADD, PDF p. 54). For a body with a hole we add to the compatibility equations conditions that the ends of such a cut match. That the two ends of the cut of the ring can differ only by a rigid-body displacement, described by six numbers, three shifts and three rotations, we prove in chapter 4, section 4.7.9. There we also show that the whole ring has a displacement field exactly when this rigid-body displacement is zero, that is, when all six numbers are zero. These are the six conditions that the hole of the ring adds to the compatibility equations. There we also say which properties of the ring the proof uses, so that it holds for every body with one hole and a cut with these properties. BARBER (PDF pp. 47-48) says the same for every hole that makes a body multiply connected: the faces of the cut have the same shape, and a rigid-body displacement with three shifts and three rotations carries one onto the other, so every such hole adds six conditions. Which hole is such? In the plane every one (SADD, PDF p. 53). In space, however, not every one. A spherical cavity leaves the body simply connected (SADD, PDF p. 53), so in it the compatibility equations are enough and the cavity adds no condition. A hole through a tube or a ring, though, makes the body multiply connected and adds six conditions. SADD (PDF pp. 53-54) writes the same conditions with sums along a curve around the hole.

With this we have answered the question from the start of the section. The six strain components cannot be arbitrary, because they come from three displacement components. We found how they are related by differentiating them twice and using the theorem on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives, which we proved with the mean value theorem used twice. On the strip with the prescribed \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = k\,y^2\) we saw that pieces with strains that do not satisfy the equations do not fit together. In a simply connected body the equations are enough, which theorem 1.137 says, and which we prove only in chapter 4. In the ring, though, we saw that they are not. When a displacement field exists, the strains in a connected body determine it up to a shift and a small rotation. We showed this by treating every segment in the body as a rigid rod and then passing from a small ball to the whole body along broken lines. In chapter 2 we turn to the forces that strain a body.
